0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
Paul wrote this letter from a Roman prison, around AD 60–62, awaiting trial before Caesar. He was chained to a guard. And from that cell he wrote what R.C. Sproul called “the most majestic letter Paul ever penned” — a letter so vast in its theological vision, so soaring in its doxology, that it feels less like correspondence and more like a window thrown open onto eternity.

The letter may have been circular — several early manuscripts omit the words “in Ephesus” from 1:1, suggesting it was passed between the churches of Asia Minor. Tychicus carried it personally (6:21). Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age — including yours.

The heartbeat phrase is in Christ, appearing over thirty times. Everything God has done, is doing, and will do for his people is located in the person of his Son. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Raised with him. Seated with him. Built together in him. The letter is not primarily about what Christians must do; it is about who Christians already are — and the doing flows from the being.

The grand theme is God’s eternal purpose to unite all things in Christ — things in heaven and things on earth (1:10). The church is not a human institution that God blesses; it is the centrepiece of his cosmic plan, the body through which the manifold wisdom of God is displayed to the watching principalities and powers (3:10). To be part of this church is to be enrolled in the most significant project in the universe.

The structure is clean and powerful. Chapters 1–3 are the great indicative: what God has done in Christ from before the foundation of the world to the present moment. Chapters 4–6 are the great imperative: how the people of God now walk, in every relationship and in every spiritual battle. The hinge is the word “therefore” in 4:1 — one of the most consequential words in Christian ethics. The imperative is always grounded in the indicative. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because we already are.

Preach this letter and you will give your congregation the full panorama of God’s saving purpose, from the eternal counsel of the Trinity before creation to the armour for the battle they face this week. There is nothing higher in Paul. There may be nothing higher in Scripture.

1.title: Grace, Election, and Prayer
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus: <sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, <sup>4</sup>even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love <sup>5</sup>he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, <sup>6</sup>to the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved. <sup>7</sup>In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace, <sup>8</sup>which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight <sup>9</sup>making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ <sup>10</sup>as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth. <sup>11</sup>In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, <sup>12</sup>so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory. <sup>13</sup>In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup>who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory. <sup>15</sup>For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, <sup>16</sup>I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, <sup>17</sup>that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, <sup>18</sup>having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, <sup>19</sup>and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might <sup>20</sup>that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, <sup>21</sup>far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. <sup>22</sup>And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, <sup>23</sup>which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens with one of the most breathtaking passages in all of Scripture — a single unbroken sentence in the Greek, 202 words long, a cascade of praise that pours out of him like a river that has broken its banks. Before a single command is given, before a single duty is laid upon the Ephesians, Paul gives them six magnificent verses of pure gift: what God has done, is doing, and will do for His people in Christ. The grammar of grace always works this way — indicative before imperative, blessing before obligation, the gift before the task. You cannot rightly obey what you have not first received.

The structure of the passage is trinitarian and it is deliberate. The Father chooses and adopts (vv.3–6); the Son redeems and reconciles (vv.7–12); the Spirit seals and guarantees (vv.13–14). Every Person of the Godhead is active in our salvation. Every blessing flows from the coordinated purpose of the triune God. And the scope is cosmic — from before the foundation of the world, when we were chosen in Christ before time began, to the fullness of time, when all things in heaven and on earth will be united in Him. We are not an afterthought in God's plan. We are its centrepiece, its showcase, the display case for the riches of His grace in the ages to come.

Count the phrase "in Christ" or "in him." It appears eleven times in twelve verses. Every single blessing — election, adoption, redemption, forgiveness, inheritance, sealing — is located not in ourselves, not in our performance, not even in our faith as such, but in Christ. We have these things because we are in Him. This is the most important prepositional phrase in the Christian life. To be in Christ is to have everything. To be outside of Christ is to have nothing, however religious, however moral, however sincere one might be. The entire letter of Ephesians is an unpacking of what it means to be in Christ — and it begins here, with a doxology so full and so free it can barely be contained in sentences.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

These twelve verses are the biblical locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of election. "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (v.4) — the election is personal, particular, and prior to anything in us. It is not based on foreseen faith; it is the ground of faith. God chose us before we existed, before we believed, before we had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). The choice was made in eternity, rooted in the sovereign good pleasure of His will (v.5), and directed toward the praise of the glory of His grace (v.6).

The purpose of election is not merely the salvation of individuals; it is the display of grace. "So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus" (2:7). We are saved so that the universe — angels, principalities, and powers — might see what grace looks like. The church is God's exhibit A: the living demonstration that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the undeserving can be made heirs, that the dead can be raised.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is not given to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance. The believer who knows they were chosen before the foundation of the world — not because of what they would become but because of God's sovereign love — has a security that no circumstance can shake. This is the pastoral gold of Ephesians 1: your standing before God does not depend on your spiritual performance today. It was settled in eternity, sealed by the Spirit, and guaranteed by the inheritance that awaits.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian Christians lived in the shadow of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, a monument to a goddess who offered fertility, protection, and blessing to her devotees. The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual elevation through initiation rites, secret knowledge, and ritual participation. Against all of this, Paul announces something infinitely more magnificent: you already possess every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places — not through ritual, not through initiation, not through any human achievement, but through your union with Christ. You have been chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, enlightened, and sealed. The goddess in the marble temple has nothing to offer you. You are already heirs of the universe.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual seeking. The bookshops are full of self-help and spirituality. People curate their own spiritual experiences, their own moral codes, their own pathways to meaning and blessing. Against all of this noise, Ephesians 1 speaks with clarifying force: every spiritual blessing is in Christ, and in Christ alone. The person who has Christ has everything. The person who lacks Christ lacks everything that ultimately matters, however enriched their life may appear. The church's task is not to offer a slightly better version of what the world already has, but to announce that in Christ, the one thing that actually satisfies every longing of the human heart is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apostolos means “sent one” — the word used for an official ambassador carrying the full authority of the one who dispatched him. The qualifier “by the will of God” is not incidental: Paul’s authority to declare the mystery of God’s purposes in chapters 2–3 rests entirely on this commission. He did not volunteer; he was made.

“Saints” (hagioi) — set-apart ones, holy ones. Not a title earned by moral achievement but a status conferred by belonging to God. In Paul’s vocabulary every believer is a saint. The word is used nine times in Ephesians; it is the community’s foundational identity before any conduct is described.

Some manuscripts omit “in Ephesus,” suggesting the letter may have circulated as a general epistle to the churches of the region. This does not diminish its authority; it extends its reach.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The standard Pauline greeting, but never merely formulaic. Charis (grace) transforms the ordinary Greek greeting chairein into a theological declaration: the entire gift of God’s undeserved favour. Eirene (peace) carries the Hebrew shalom: not the absence of conflict but the positive flourishing of a life rightly ordered to God.

The double source — “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” — places Father and Son on the same grammatical and theological level as the single origin of both gifts. Casual Trinitarian theology, stated before the letter has even begun.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three uses of the blessing root (eulogeo / eulogia) in one verse: God is to be blessed (praised) because he has blessed (given) us. The blessings are “spiritual” — not meaning immaterial, but coming from and consisting in the Holy Spirit. “Every” spiritual blessing: not some, not the ones we have earned, but the entire treasury. The word “in Christ” will govern the entire doxology: every blessing is located in him, accessible only through union with him.

It is worth slowing down on the word itself, because the whole doxology turns on it. To bless (Greek eulogeo, literally “to speak well of” — from eu, well, and logos, word) is to speak a good word over someone. But it means two very different things depending on who is speaking. When we bless God, we cannot add a single thing to the One who already holds all good in himself; our blessing can only be praise — the glad acknowledgement of the good he is and has done, speaking well of him because he is worthy of it. When God blesses us, his word is never mere breath. For God, to speak good over someone is to do good to them: his blessing does not merely wish us well, it makes us well, bestowing the very thing it names. It was so from the first page — “God blessed them and said, Be fruitful” (Gen. 1:28) — where the word carried the gift it spoke. So Paul’s sentence swings on a hinge: we bless God with our lips because he has first blessed us with his hand.

One distinction guards against a common confusion. The “Blessed” of “Blessed be God” (eulogetos) is not the “blessed” of the Beatitudes (makarios). Makarios describes the happy, flourishing, God-favoured state of a person — blessed are the poor in spirit. Eulogetos is reserved in the New Testament for God alone, the One worthy to be praised. English blurs the two into one word; the Greek keeps them apart.

“Heavenly places” (epouraniois) is a phrase unique to Ephesians (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). It describes the realm of spiritual reality where the decisive events occur and from which the decisive blessings flow. The Christian’s life is simultaneously earthly and heavenly — the blessings are already fully given in the heavenly realm even while they are being worked out on earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before creation, before time, before any human could earn or forfeit it, God chose his people in Christ. The ground of that choice lies entirely in God — not foreseen faith or merit, but his own free love.

And he chose us for something: “that we should be holy and blameless before him.” Holy (Greek hagios) means set apart — as the Temple vessels were holy, reserved wholly for God’s use. To be chosen holy is first to belong to him, and that belonging reshapes everything: how we think, what we love, how we live (cf. 1 Pet. 1:15–16). Blameless (amōmos) is the word for a sacrifice without blemish, fit to be offered — standing before God with no charge held against us. And the crucial phrase is “before him”: blameless in God’s sight, not our own.

Does Paul mean sinless perfection? Many read these words and feel condemned rather than called. He means two things at once. Now, by imputation, you are already holy and blameless in God’s sight — not on your record but clothed in Christ’s (Col. 1:22). The believer still fighting sin is no less blameless, because the blamelessness counted is Christ’s. And one day, by transformation, God will finish what he began, presenting you without stumbling before his glory (Jude 24; 1 John 3:2).

Hold both together. The standing gives you your footing — “God sees me in Christ; I am not disqualified.” The trajectory gives you your direction — “this is where he is taking me; I am not finished.” So the believer who sinned badly this week does not come to God with a diminished holiness, for his holiness was never measured by this week. You can return without first making yourself presentable, because Christ has already made you so — not a licence to sin (Rom. 6:1–2), but the mercy that makes repentance possible.

But a sermon on this verse always raises two questions, and a congregation is right to ask them. If God chose before we had done anything, is that fair to those he did not choose? And if the choice was his, what becomes of mine — and why evangelise at all? Take them honestly. The fairness question quietly assumes we were owed a choosing; we were not. Left to justice, every one of us would be passed by, for all had sinned and earned the same judgment (Rom. 3:23; 6:23). The marvel of this verse is not that some are not chosen but that any are — that grace should reach into a mass of the justly condemned and lift out a people who deserved exactly what the rest received. No one perishes who wanted Christ and was refused; the lost are lost by their own will, the saved rescued by God’s.

As for your own choosing, Scripture holds both truths without apology and so must we. The same letter that says you were chosen before the foundation of the world will plead with you to walk worthy of your calling (4:1); the same Paul who wrote this begged men, as though God were making his appeal through him, to be reconciled to God (2 Cor. 5:20). Election never turns you into a stone. You heard, you believed, and your believing was truly your own (v. 13) — God’s sovereignty runs underneath your real choice, not instead of it. Where the two meet is a depth we are not given to sound: the secret things belong to the Lord our God (Deut. 29:29), and when Paul reached this very wall he did not climb it but asked who we are to answer back to God (Rom. 9:20). And far from killing mission, this doctrine is the only reason mission cannot fail — it was to a discouraged evangelist in a hostile city that the Lord said, “I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:9–10). We preach to all, freely and urgently, precisely because he has a people to gather, and not one of them will be missed.

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In love” almost certainly modifies predestination rather than what precedes: it was in love that he predestined. Predestination is not cold decree but the Father’s affectionate purpose to have children. The warmth of the word “adoption” confirms it.

“Adoption” (huiothesia) is a legal term for the full conferral of sonship on someone not born to it. Roman adoption was irrevocable and conferred complete inheritance rights. The adopted son had all the standing of a biological heir — the past could not reclaim him. “According to the purpose of his will” — the ground is entirely within God. This is not a harsh doctrine; it is the guarantee of its permanence.

And yet no doctrine is more likely to send a tender conscience into fear, for the moment election is preached someone asks: how do I know that I am one of them — and what if I am not? The mistake, and it is a common one, is to try to climb up into heaven and read the secret book of God’s decree, as though assurance were found by prying into what he has kept in his own hand. You cannot read it, and you were never asked to. God has not hidden the evidence in eternity; he has laid it down here, within your reach, in his Son. So do not look up into the hidden counsel; look at Christ, and look at your own heart’s answer to him. Do you want him? Do you find yourself — however feebly, however unevenly — trusting him, loving his people, grieved when you sin against him? That desire did not begin with you. Dead men do not long for God; the very wanting is the fingerprint of the Spirit who sealed you when you believed (v. 13). Faith is not the ticket you must produce to prove you were chosen; it is the evidence that you were. So the anxious believer should stop searching the sky for a name he cannot see and look instead at the cross he already loves. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37) — and the proof that you were chosen before the foundation of the world is the plainest thing in the world: you came.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of three “to the praise of his glory” refrains (vv. 6, 12, 14), marking the three Trinitarian movements of the doxology. Every section ends at the same destination: God praised. Salvation has a design beyond the saved.

“The Beloved” — a title for Christ that echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism (“This is my beloved Son”) and the transfiguration. The blessings come to us because we are in the one who is supremely loved. We receive what belongs to him because we are in him.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Redemption” (apolutrosis) is the language of the slave market and the exodus: the payment of a price to secure release. The price is specific: his blood. Not his teaching, not his example, not his moral influence — his blood. Forgiveness is the content of what redemption achieves: the actual cancellation of actual sins.

“According to the riches of his grace” — not the minimum, not the merely adequate, but proportioned to the wealth of God’s own grace. This is a lavish transaction, not a careful one. (cf. Col. 1:14; 1 Pet. 1:18–19)

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Lavished” — poured out abundantly, overflowing. God did not give grace carefully, measuring out precisely what was sufficient. He poured. The grace is not sentimental, however: it was given “in all wisdom and insight” — with full knowledge of what we are and what we need. The lavishness and the wisdom belong together: it is not reckless giving but intelligent abundance.

But a careful reader will stop and ask whose wisdom and insight this is, and it is exactly the right question. Read as above, it is God’s: he gave wisely. Many readers, however, have always instinctively heard it the other way — that the wisdom and insight are part of what he lavished on us — and that instinct has strong support.

Notice first what the two words are, because they are not synonyms. Sophia is wisdom in the deep sense: the grasp of how things actually are, of God and his purposes. Phronesis is its practical cousin — prudence, discernment, the working out of that grasp in real decisions. One sees; the other knows what to do on Monday morning. Paul does not choose between them. He says grace was poured out in all of both.

Three things point toward these being given to us. The nearest parallel is the twin letter, where Paul prays that the Colossians be “filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (Col. 1:9) — plainly a gift to believers. Second, Paul prays for precisely this a few verses further on, that God would give them “a spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened” (vv. 17–18): the same gift, now asked for outright. Third, and most tellingly, the sentence runs straight on into what follows — he lavished grace on us in all wisdom and insight, making known to us the mystery of his will (v. 9). A mystery cannot be made known to someone who has not been given the faculty to receive it. The wisdom is the equipment for the revelation arriving in the very next breath.

And nothing is lost if a reader takes it the other way, because both are true. God’s plan is supremely wise, and Paul will say so outright: through the church the manifold wisdom of God is now made known even to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (3:10). But the point to carry away is this. The grace that saves you does not rescue you and then leave you standing there baffled about what has happened to you. He gives the gift, and then he gives the eyes to see the gift. That is precisely why this letter can spend three chapters unfolding the eternal purposes of God and still expect ordinary people in Ephesus — dockworkers, slaves, tradesmen — to follow every word of it.

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “mystery” (mystērion) is not a puzzle but a plan once hidden and now disclosed — how God would deal with sin, unite divided humanity, and bring all creation under one head. What was concealed for ages has now been unveiled in Christ (cf. Rom. 16:25–26).

And God’s ultimate purpose is caught in a single towering Greek word: anakephalaiōsis — to sum up, to gather everything under one head. The fall shattered a unified world: God and humanity estranged, people at war with one another, creation groaning under the curse (Rom. 8:20–22), the very powers in rebellion. God’s plan, purposed before creation, is to reunite it all — “things in heaven and things on earth” — under the one true head, Jesus Christ.

Notice Paul says all things, not merely all people — ta panta, the whole of what exists. His salvation is bigger than the rescue of individual souls out of a ruined world; it is the restoration of everything to its right relation with its true head. The material creation is not discarded but renewed, for Christ’s risen body is the prototype (Rev. 21:1–5). Even the hostile spiritual powers are brought into subjection, already disarmed at the cross (Col. 2:15; 1 Cor. 15:24–28). “In him all things hold together” (Col. 1:17) — and what he now sustains he will one day visibly, gloriously order under himself.

All of this waits for “the fullness of time,” God’s appointed moment (cf. Gal. 4:4–5). So you are not adrift in a random universe sliding toward chaos. You live inside a plan conceived before creation, secured at the cross, moving surely toward the day when every broken thing — every ruined relationship, every groaning creature, every rebel power — is gathered up and healed under Christ.

All of that is true, and it can still hover a foot above the ground. So let it come down. What would it actually look like for everything to be gathered under one head?

Measure the promise against what is broken now. A world under one head is a world where the ground no longer throws up thorns and the body no longer throws up tumours; where there are no funerals, because there is nothing left to bury. It is a world with no borders and no armies, because there is nothing left to defend against; where families are not quietly divided by something said twenty years ago; where you no longer have to manage the distance between people who used to be close. It is a world in which you are no longer divided against yourself — where the man you want to be and the man you are have at last become the same man (cf. Rom. 7:19). And it is a world where heaven and earth are no longer two addresses. Just now we pray that God’s will be done on earth as it is in heaven (Matt. 6:10) — a prayer that quietly admits a gap. Then the gap closes: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Rev. 21:3). And nothing good is lost on the way: the glory and the honour of the nations are carried in (Rev. 21:24–26). Everything you have ever loved is kept; everything that spoiled it is gone.

Now, or later? Both — and holding the two together is what keeps you from either despair or pretence. Already: Christ has been raised and seated above every rule and authority, and given as head over all things to the church (1:20–22, only a few verses away); the powers were disarmed at the cross (Col. 2:15). The gathering has begun, and it has a visible address. That is why Paul can say that through the church the manifold wisdom of God is now made known even to the powers (3:10). When a Jew and a Gentile sat down at one table in Ephesus, that was not good community relations; it was the future arriving early, a patch of the reunited world showing through the old one. Every genuine reconciliation in a congregation is the same thing. Not yet: “at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see Jesus” (Heb. 2:8–9). That is the honest Christian position. The world is plainly not yet under his feet, and we are not asked to pretend otherwise. We see him; that is enough to go on with.

And why does this matter so much to God? Because the fall was, at its root, a dishonouring. It was creatures declining to be governed in the world their Maker made, glory handed to things that never made anything, the name of God treated as negotiable in his own house. Sin is not merely damage; it is a rival throne. So the summing up of all things under Christ is the ending of every rival throne — not one rebel province left, not one corner of reality still ordered to something other than the glory of the One who made it, until every knee bows and every tongue confesses to the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:10–11). Which is precisely why this passage keeps returning to one refrain: to the praise of his glory (vv. 6, 12, 14). The uniting is not an end in itself. It exists so that God is at last, and everywhere, honoured as what he actually is.

And this, if you have ever felt it, is the world you already want. The ache underneath our best music and our worst politics is the same ache: we keep trying to build a world that holds together, and we keep failing, because every attempt unites it under something that cannot carry the weight — a leader, a nation, an idea, a self. You have been homesick for a country you have never visited. That homesickness is not a defect in you. It is the memory of what the world was for and the promise of what it will be — and Paul here tells you its name. Not a system and not a golden age, but a Person, under whom everything finally fits.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In him we have obtained an inheritance.” Everything in this doxology has hung on those two small words — in him. Paul has used them again and again: chosen in him (v.4), adopted in him (v.5), redeemed in him (v.7), and now given an inheritance in him. They describe the believer’s entire standing before God: not in your own name or on your own record, but clothed in Christ, accepted because he is accepted. When the Father looks at you, he sees you in his beloved Son — and loves you with the very love he bears the Son (John 17:23; Col. 3:3). Let that settle.

The word for inheritance, eklērōthēmen, means to be allotted a portion, as the land was parcelled out to Israel (Josh. 14:1–2). And it runs two ways. First, God himself is our portion — as the Levites received no land because the Lord was their inheritance (Num. 18:20; Ps. 16:5–6). The inheritance is finally not a list of gifts but the Giver: “God is my portion forever” (Ps. 73:26). Second, it is the glory still to come — “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet. 1:4), for we are “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). Granted now, fully received on the last day.

And it cannot miscarry, because God “works all things according to the counsel of his will” — not some things, not most, but all; not reacting to events but unfolding his own eternal purpose. The God who works all things is the God who has promised you the inheritance. It will be delivered.

Both halves of that inheritance deserve more than a sentence, because between them they are the whole of what you are promised.

Take the first: God himself as your portion. Picture the day the land was divided. Eleven tribes walk away holding a map — this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces, the well. Levi is handed nothing at all. No acres, no boundary stones, no deed. To any watching eye the priestly tribe has been cheated, and then God says the sentence that explains everything: I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel (Num. 18:20). The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God. And the whole nation was meant to look at that one landless tribe, generation after generation, and learn what wealth actually is.

Test it on yourself, because it is testable. Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted — your health returned, every broken relationship mended, the people you have buried given back, no more grief anywhere — and God himself were not there. Would that be heaven? Every Christian who has thought about it honestly knows the answer is no. Which is exactly the psalmist’s point: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Ps. 73:25). And the reverse is just as true, and far more comforting: if you had him and nothing else, you would still be rich. That is why this portion cannot be lost. Everything else you own can be taken from you by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply by time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed.

Now the second half, the glory still to come, which is usually left vague and should not be. Scripture gives it real content. A body — raised imperishable, no longer failing, transformed to be like his own glorious body (1 Cor. 15:42–44; Phil. 3:21). A world — not a wisp of cloud but new heavens and a new earth, and the astonishing promise that the meek inherit it (Matt. 5:5; Rev. 21:1–5). A face — “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2), “they will see his face” (Rev. 22:4), which is the one thing Moses asked for and was not given. A likeness — we shall be like him, the divided self finally and permanently healed. And work worth doing, with real authority in a world that no longer resists it (Luke 19:17). Then notice the measure Paul’s companion text puts on all of it: we are “fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). Not a modest plot at the edge of the estate. Whatever belongs to the Son is what is being settled on you.

And the two halves are not rivals; they are one thing. The coming glory is simply having him with nothing left in the way — no sin, no distance, no dying, no dullness of heart — together with everything he has made new. So read the verb again, and note its tense: we have obtained an inheritance. Not may yet, not hope to. The allotment is already made and the deed already signed in the blood of the Son; only the delivery is still outstanding. Which means the poorest believer reading this page is, at this moment, an heir of God — and the estate is not in doubt, because the One who works all things according to the counsel of his will is the executor of the will.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You also” — now the Gentiles. The same election, the same redemption, the same sealing. The Spirit is the seal: in antiquity a seal conveyed ownership, authenticity, and security. God has stamped his ownership on every believer. The Spirit cannot be revoked; the ownership stands.

The Spirit is also the arrabōn — the guarantee, the down payment, the first instalment of the full inheritance still to come. What the Spirit gives now is not the whole but the taste, the proof, the pledge of everything that is coming. The “until” is eschatological: the Spirit holds the believer sealed until the day the full possession is received. (cf. Rom. 8:16; 2 Cor. 1:22)

Both of those words — sealed, guarantee — have gone flat with age, and they are far too good to leave flat. Put them back on the dock at Ephesus.

A merchant’s cargo is loaded and bound, and before the ship sails he presses his signet ring into hot wax across the bindings. Every man on that quay could read what the mark meant, and it said three things at once. This is mine — ownership, hands off. This is genuine — not a substitute swapped in along the way, but the real consignment. And this is protected — because the cargo now crosses hostile water and strange customs houses, and to break that seal is not to quarrel with a crate; it is to answer to the man whose ring made the mark. Now hear what Paul says God has stamped on you. Not wax, and not a certificate. The seal is a Person: you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit. God’s own answer to the question of whether you will arrive is to place himself on you.

Notice also when it happened, because it matters to any reader who has wondered whether he has missed something. Paul ties it to a single moment: you heard, you believed, you were sealed. Not a later upgrade for advanced Christians, not a second blessing that some receive and others wait for — dear brothers and sisters do read it that way, and they read it out of a genuine hunger for more of God, which is nothing to sneer at. But the grammar here runs the other way. If you have believed, you are sealed already. And you can check it, not by hunting for a feeling, but by looking for the marks the Spirit actually leaves: that you call God Father and mean it (Rom. 8:15–16), that sin now grieves you where once it did not trouble you at all, that Christ has become precious to you rather than merely true.

Then the second word. The arrabōn was a legal down payment — and in Greek to this day the same word means an engagement ring. That is the picture. Not a souvenir, not a token to remember him by, but a first instalment that legally commits the giver to pay the rest. And here is the thing most people miss about a deposit: it is not a sample of some different substance. It is the first portion of the very same thing. So what you have of the Spirit now is not a lesser commodity than heaven; it is heaven’s first payment, in heaven’s own currency. That unaccountable peace that arrived when nothing in your circumstances justified it; the joy that has caught you sideways in a hymn; the love you find you have for people you would never have chosen — that is not preparation for the inheritance. It is the inheritance, in instalment.

Which also explains why the Christian life feels the way it does. You hold the deposit, not the estate. So the ache is not a sign that something has gone wrong with your faith; the deposit was designed to make you homesick. A man with an engagement ring is not less eager for the wedding than a man without one — he is far more eager, and far more certain. And note who stands to lose if the day never comes: the one who paid the earnest money. God has put down a deposit he does not intend to forfeit.

So the doxology closes as it has twice already: to the praise of his glory (vv. 6, 12, 14). Three times, and each time after a different Person has done his work — the Father choosing, the Son redeeming, the Spirit sealing. One salvation, three hands, one refrain. God has not handed you a receipt for the inheritance and left you to wait. He has given you the first instalment of it, and the first instalment is himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul prays. The man who has just outlined the most concentrated doctrinal statement in the New Testament now falls on his knees for the people he loves. And his prayer is not for comfort, not for prosperity, not even for their safety — it is for illumination. He prays that they would know. Not know more information about God — they have just received an overwhelming cascade of theological truth. But know it experientially, vitally, in the way that transforms the soul rather than merely informing the mind. There is a vast difference between possessing a treasure and being fully aware of what you possess. Paul prays to close that gap.

Three things he asks for illumination about, each one more staggering than the last. First: the hope of their calling — the glorious future that God has promised and secured for those who are in Christ. Second: the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints — the almost incomprehensible truth that God Himself regards His people as His inheritance, His treasure, His glory. Third: the immeasurable greatness of His power toward those who believe. And to give the Ephesians a sense of how great that power is, Paul reaches for the most powerful event in history as his measure: the resurrection of Jesus from the dead and His exaltation to the right hand of the Father, far above every name and authority and power in the universe. That power — the power that raised the dead and shattered the dominion of death — is at work in you.

The prayer closes with a vision of Christ as head over all things for the church, which is His body, the fullness of the One who fills all in all. The church is not a voluntary association of like-minded believers. It is the body of the cosmic Lord, the community through which the exalted Christ exercises His reign in the world. To be part of the church is to be part of the most significant institution in the universe — the community of the risen King.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for "the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him" (v.17). This single phrase encapsulates the Reformed understanding of how divine truth moves from the page to the heart. The Spirit who inspired the Scripture is also required to illuminate the reader of Scripture. Without the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, the words of God remain external — true, but not transforming; known about, but not known. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: the Scripture needs no external proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces the certainty of it in the heart of the believer.

The practical implication is that Bible reading and prayer are inseparable disciplines. To open the Scripture without asking the Spirit to open our eyes to it is to work without our most essential tool. The Puritans understood this: they typically spent as much time in prayer before Bible reading as in the reading itself, asking God to grant illumination. The eyes of the heart do not open themselves. This prayer of Paul's is therefore not only a prayer about the Ephesians — it is a prayer for every reader of Scripture in every age who wants not merely to know about God but to know God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians; he cannot lay hands on them; he cannot preach to them in person. What he can do is pray — and his prayer from chains is not for his own release but for their illumination. This is one of the most searching things in the letter: the imprisoned apostle, whose situation would seem to give him every right to focus on his own needs, pours his intercession entirely outward, toward the people he loves. His joy is in their knowledge of Christ, not in his own circumstances. This is the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:5) applied to prayer.

Now: We live in an age of unprecedented access to biblical content. More sermons, commentaries, podcasts, and Bible apps exist today than at any point in history. And yet spiritual blindness remains our greatest problem. We have more information about God than any previous generation, and arguably less experiential knowledge of Him. Paul's prayer cuts through all of this: what we need is not more content but opened eyes — the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, granting us not information but encounter. The Ephesians had Paul's letter. We have the whole Bible. Both of us need the same thing: the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For this reason” looks back over the whole doxology: because of all God has done in Christ, Paul prays. Theology fuels intercession. The man who has just spent fourteen verses gazing at the riches of grace can do nothing else but fall to his knees — prayer rising from a mind filled with God, not an anxious heart out of options.

Notice what he does. A prisoner in Rome, writing to a church he may never see again, his first response is not to instruct or correct but to pray — and “I do not cease,” he says. He carries these believers before God continually, because he knows the one thing they most need is the one thing no letter can give: for God himself to open their eyes.

He gives thanks for two things held together — their “faith in the Lord Jesus” and their “love toward all the saints.” It is always both. Genuine faith never stays private; it reaches out to the people Christ loves. Faith looks up to Christ; love reaches out to his body — “faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6; cf. 1 John 4:20–21). And he begins with thanks, not with what they lack: grateful sufficiency reaching for more, not anxious need grasping for it.

Stand where he is standing as he writes this. Paul is in Rome under guard, most likely chained at the wrist to a soldier who is relieved every few hours. He has no freedom to travel, no money to send, no authority to step in and sort anything out in Ephesus, and a real possibility that he will never see these people again in this life. Word has reached him — somebody has come up the road with a report about them — and what he does with that report is the whole point. He cannot get to them. So he does the only thing left to him, and it turns out to be the greatest thing one person can ever do for another: he carries them to God. Prison did not reduce his ministry to prayer. Prison revealed that prayer had always been the larger half of it.

And pause on how he knows anything at all: I have heard of your faith. Someone talked. A traveller, a merchant, a courier mentioned a church in Ephesus where people believed in Jesus and looked after each other, and the news travelled far enough to reach a cell in Rome. Your faith is being reported somewhere too, and usually to people you will never meet. You are rarely the best judge of what your own quiet obedience is doing at a distance.

Then weigh what he actually gives thanks for, because in one line he has sketched the whole letter: faith in the Lord Jesus, and love toward all the saints. Do not slide past that little word. Not love toward the saints you would have chosen. Ephesus was a room containing Jews and Gentiles together — people raised to regard one another as unclean, who now had to pass the same cup — and Paul is about to spend an entire chapter on how that dividing wall came down (2:14–16). So this is not warmth toward the agreeable. It is love toward the whole awkward set of them, the ones you would cross the street to avoid included, which is the only kind of love that proves anything at all. Faith looks up to Christ; love looks sideways at the people he died for and calls them family.

And he starts with thanksgiving. He has plenty he could correct, and he will get to it; but the first thing out of his mouth about this church is gratitude to God for what is already there. That is worth copying the next time you think about a person, or a congregation, who has a long way still to go.

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul addresses God as “the Father of glory” — glory being the Hebrew kābôd, weight, substance: God is the most real thing that exists, and everything else has weight only as a reflection of his. To call him “Father of glory” is to say glory is not something he occasionally has; it is what he is. Paul worships before he asks a thing.

Then he asks — for “a Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.” Not a second giving of the Spirit; the Ephesians already have him (v.13). He asks that the Spirit would function as the one who illumines — taking what is already true of God and making it personally, penetratingly known. Wisdom is the capacity to see reality as God sees it: to read your suffering in the frame of his purpose, to see the cross — apparent defeat — as the pivot of history. Revelation is not new Scripture but the curtain drawn back on what is already given, so the words you have read for years suddenly land with new weight, as if seen for the first time.

And it all has one target: “the knowledge of him.” The Greek is epignōsis — full, personal, experiential knowing; not knowledge about God but knowledge of him. Paul could have prayed for their circumstances to ease, their numbers to grow. He prays instead that they would know God — because the one who truly knows him has everything he needs for anything he will face (cf. John 17:3; Phil. 3:10).

Take that word glory down off the shelf for a moment, because it has become a church word and it began as an ordinary one. The Hebrew kābôd means weight — heaviness, substance, the thing that is solid enough to matter. Which quietly reverses how we normally rank the world. The things that feel most solid to us are the things we can bank, insure and put on a CV: the salary, the house, the reputation, the career. Scripture calls those the lightweight things, the ones that blow away (Ps. 1:4). God is the heavy thing. He is the most real object in existence, and everything else has weight only in the measure that it reflects him. To call him the Father of glory is to say that this weight is not something he sometimes carries. It is what he is.

Now notice something easy to miss, and it is the most striking thing in the verse. Paul has just written the most magnificent fourteen verses in the New Testament. He is the apostle; the words are inspired; the doctrine is flawless. And he does not assume for a moment that this will be enough. He stops and prays — because he knows he can put the truth in front of their minds and still not get it into their hearts. Only God can open eyes. Every preacher and every parent learns this eventually, usually the hard way: you can explain something perfectly and watch it not land, and you have no lever for the last six inches. Paul knew it from the start, and so the greatest teacher in the church turns immediately into an intercessor.

Which tells you what kind of thing is being asked for here. Not information — that you can go and get. You can read the commentary, take the course, learn the Greek, and still not know him, in the same way you can know a man’s birthday, his job, the town he grew up in and the name of his dog, and have never once met him. That is the difference epignōsis is reaching for. So run the test on yourself honestly: is God someone you know a great deal about, or someone you know? The two feel similar from the inside for a long time, and they are not remotely the same.

And if the honest answer is the first one, the verse itself tells you what to do about it, because it is a prayer and not an instruction. You cannot manufacture this; you can ask for it. So ask — for yourself, in these words, this week. Paul could have prayed that their circumstances would ease or their numbers would swell. He asked instead that they would know God, because a man who truly knows him is already equipped for anything that is coming, and a man who does not is unequipped for everything, however well his life is currently going.

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The eyes of your hearts” — in Scripture the heart is not mainly the seat of feeling but the centre of the whole person, and it has its own eyes. You can have perfect eyesight and be spiritually blind; you can understand every word of a sentence and miss what it means. That is why Paul prays rather than merely explains: illumination is a gift, and the Spirit who inspired the word must open the eyes that read it.

He prays they would see three things. First, “the hope to which he has called you.” Biblical hope is not a wish but a certainty not yet visible (elpis) — the whole future God has promised: the resurrection of the body, the renewal of all things, the end of every grief, the face-to-face knowledge of God, all guaranteed because Jesus rose. It is possible to be a real Christian and still live as though this life were all there is — grieving without comfort, fearing death as if resurrection were not real. The heart that has truly seen this hope holds the present loosely and can endure loss without being destroyed (Heb. 6:19; 1 Pet. 1:3).

Second, “the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints” — and the preposition stops you. This is God’s inheritance in his people, not theirs in him. Paul is saying the unthinkable: God has an inheritance, and it is us. We are his treasure — as he once said of Israel, “you shall be my treasured possession” (Exod. 19:5; Deut. 7:6). And it is glorious, not because of what we are now — still broken, still being sanctified — but because of what we will be when Christ presents us to the Father, radiant with his own glory (Jude 24). Jesus is glorified in his people (John 17:10). The God of the universe calls you his inheritance, and he will not lose you.

Take that first phrase slowly, because it names something you have probably experienced without having a word for it. The eyes of the heart are the difference between reading a sentence and seeing it. Every Christian knows the strange moment when a verse he has read a hundred times — and could have quoted accurately on any of those hundred occasions — suddenly opens, and he finds himself sitting very still over words that did nothing to him last year. Nothing changed in the text. The lights came on in the room. That is precisely what Paul is asking God for, and it is why he prays rather than simply explaining himself more clearly. He can raise the standard of the teaching; he cannot reach in and flip the switch.

Then the hope. Paul’s own picture for it is an anchor (Heb. 6:19), and the picture repays getting right, because an anchor does not work the way we tend to imagine. It is not dropped behind the ship to hold her to where she has already been. It is thrown out ahead, it grips ground the crew cannot see, and it steadies them in the water they are in now. Christian hope is not nostalgia and it is not optimism. It is certainty about what lies ahead, sunk into ground not yet visible, doing its work in this week’s weather. And whether you have truly seen it tends to show up in three very ordinary places: what happens inside you when money goes, what happens inside you at a graveside, and whether the thought of your own death is a horror or a door.

Now the second thing, which is the one to carry home. God has an inheritance, and it is his people. Sit with what that sentence has to mean. He already owns everything; the galaxies are not his estate but his handiwork, and he could speak a thousand more into being before breakfast. So what does the God who owns it all count as treasure — what did he go out and purchase at cost? Not the stars. You. Jesus told a story about a man who found treasure hidden in a field and sold all that he had to buy that field (Matt. 13:44), and we have usually read it with ourselves as the buyer. Turn it round and read it again. He is the man who sold everything.

And any treasure can be priced by what the buyer was willing to pay. Peter gives the figure: you were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18–19). That is what God reckoned his inheritance to be worth. So when you are tempted — as most believers are by about Tuesday — to think of yourself as someone God barely tolerates, a nuisance he puts up with for Jesus’ sake, this verse stands squarely in the way. You are not what he tolerates. You are what he is inheriting.

And Paul is not finished. There is a third thing he wants them to see, and it meets the obvious objection to everything just said — that people like us are far too weak to make it to the end. That is the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul piles up four Greek words for power: dynamis (capacity to act), energeia (power at work), kratos (power that prevails), ischus (raw strength). No single word will do; he heaps them together like a man describing something beyond description — and then anchors the whole pile to one event: the resurrection and exaltation of Christ. If you want to know the scale of what God will exert for those who believe, look at the empty tomb.

But power for what? Not, mostly, for spectacle. It is power to believe and keep believing, for even faith is God’s work in us (Phil. 2:13); power over sin, since the strength that broke death can break the grip of an old habit (Rom. 6:4–6); power to endure — the long marriage, the chronic illness, the prayer carried for years — “strengthened with all power… for all endurance and patience with joy” (Col. 1:11); power to love the difficult and ungrateful, which no natural temperament supplies (Eph. 3:16–17); and power in weakness, “made perfect” precisely when human strength has run out (2 Cor. 12:9).

And it is worth saying what this power is not for. Not to remove all hardship — the man writing this prayer is in prison, his thorn unremoved; his power was given for endurance, not escape (2 Cor. 12:7–9). And not as a reward for impressive faith: it is toward “us who believe,” not us who believe flawlessly. “I believe; help my unbelief!” cried a desperate father — and Jesus acted (Mark 9:24). The power does not scale with the strength of your faith but with the strength of God, unlocked by any faith, however weak, fixed on the right object. Its aim is not to make your outer life spectacular but to make your inner life increasingly like the Son’s — and that is exactly what Paul is praying for.

Now come back to the measurement, because it is the most extraordinary thing in the sentence and the easiest to read straight past. Paul does not say that God’s power is like resurrection power, or reminiscent of it, or a scaled-down domestic version of it for household use. He says it is according to the working of the might God exerted in Christ when he raised him from the dead — the same exertion, the identical output, now aimed in your direction. He has handed you a measuring stick and told you plainly what it measures.

So look hard at what that power had to do the first time it was used. This was not a resuscitation, not a man caught at the edge whose heart had stopped a few minutes earlier. Jesus had been executed in public by professionals who did that work for a living and did not make mistakes about it. He had been dead long enough to be taken down, wrapped, carried, and sealed in. The case was closed. The stone was in place, the guard was posted, and his friends had gone home to make arrangements for grief, not for Sunday. Death had won completely, publicly, with witnesses. And then God exerted himself, and the strongest thing in this world — the one power that has never yet lost an argument with anybody — simply gave way.

Now set your own situation down beside that. The habit you have failed to break for twenty years. The person you cannot forgive and have quietly stopped pretending you can. The fear you have reasoned with a hundred times and never once beaten. The prayer you have carried so long that you no longer really expect anything to come of it. Ask the one question this verse is built to make you ask: is any of it harder than a corpse? That is the comparison Paul has deliberately set up. Whatever is still holding out in you is not stronger than death — and death is precisely what this power has already beaten, once, in the open, in front of everyone.

Notice too the small word toward. It is a direction, not a location. This power is not sitting in a vault with your name on a form you have to fill in correctly before anything is released; it is aimed at you and already in motion — toward us who believe. Which is also why it comes third in the prayer, and why it answers the objection every honest reader has been quietly forming since verse 18. The hope tells you where you are going. The inheritance tells you what you are worth to him. And then, just as you think that people like you will never actually arrive, comes the power — and it is measured by an empty tomb.

And there is one more proof, which Paul will spell out within a few paragraphs. The same power has already been used on you: “even when we were dead in our trespasses, [God] made us alive together with Christ… and raised us up with him” (2:5–6). You were not merely assisted or encouraged. You were raised. So the question of whether this power is equal to your situation has already been settled in your own case, on the day you first believed. It has done the hardest thing it will ever be asked to do for you — and it did that while you were dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion” — and then, as if the list were not enough, “above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.” Every hierarchy, every power, in this world and the next: there is no category of existence in which Christ does not hold the supreme place.

To us this can feel like an abstraction. To the Ephesians it was liberation. Their city was saturated with spiritual power — the temple of Artemis, and a whole magic industry (when Paul preached, new converts burned scrolls worth fifty thousand pieces of silver, Acts 19:19). They lived in dread of named powers — spirits and rulers that governed life and had to be appeased. Into that fear Paul announces: Christ is above every one of them. Every name you fear, every power you tried to placate, is under the feet of the one who saved you.

He is drawing on the whole sweep of Scripture — the Messiah seated at God’s right hand (Ps. 110:1), the Son of Man given everlasting dominion (Dan. 7:13–14), the name above every name (Phil. 2:9–11). And at the cross, which looked like defeat, “he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Col. 2:15). They still operate, still oppose (6:12) — but as defeated enemies, not sovereign lords. There is a vast difference between a roaring lion and a reigning one (1 Pet. 5:8). And “not only in this age but the one to come” seals it: his lordship is not provisional, awaiting review. The end of history will simply unveil what is already true.

R.C. Sproul used to say the most important question is not what you think of yourself but what you think of Christ — because how large he is in your thinking determines how small everything else becomes. The believer who grasps this does not live under the tyranny of others’ opinion, or the news cycle, or the apparent strength of evil, for every one of those powers operates under Christ’s permission. As Alistair Begg has put it, the church need not wring its hands over who is in the White House, because it knows who is on the throne. And if you feel the enemy’s attacks and wonder whether the darkness will win — the power pressing against you has a commander, that commander is already defeated, and you belong to the one who defeated him.

Two details in the wording repay a closer look, and both sharpen the comfort.

The first is the small word far. Paul does not simply write that Christ is above these powers; he reaches for an emphatic compound, hyperanō — far above, high over. And that is a claim about kind, not merely about rank. He is not the highest name on the chart, the senior officer at the top of a chain of command that also contains the others. He is not on the chart at all. He is the one who drew it. Which is also why the four words Paul heaps up — rule, authority, power, dominion — are better heard as the ranks and titles of a hierarchy than as four synonyms for “strong things”. He is reciting the whole table of organisation, top to bottom, and putting the entire structure under one pair of feet. Nor are these merely human offices: in this letter such powers are spiritual before they are political (3:10; 6:12), which is exactly why he will later insist that our struggle is not against flesh and blood. The visible authorities that trouble us have invisible backing.

The second detail is sharper still: above every name that is named. In Ephesus that was not poetry; it was an attack on an industry. In the ancient magical world, power lived in names. The whole apparatus worked by knowing the right name and pronouncing it correctly — the city’s formulae were famous enough across the empire to have a nickname, the Ephesian letters. To know a spirit’s name was to gain leverage over it. Which is why the scene Luke records in that same city lands so hard: the seven sons of Sceva tried to use “Jesus whom Paul proclaims” as one more name in the toolkit, and were beaten out of the house by the very man they were attempting to help (Acts 19:13–16). The name of Jesus is not a lever to be operated. He is a Lord to be belonged to. And that, rather than any technique, is why the converts made a bonfire of their scrolls a few verses later. When you have the Person, you no longer need the formulae.

You have your own names. They are not Artemis, and you have never bought a scroll, but you can usually identify them by asking what you find yourself appeasing — the market, the algorithm, the scan result, the mortgage, the opinion of people whose approval you have never actually enjoyed. We do not burn incense to such things. We simply organise our lives around them and lie awake for them, which is the same transaction conducted more discreetly. Every one of them is named in this verse, and every one of them is under his feet.

And the final clause quietly removes their future as well: not only in this age but also in the one to come. Every power that has ever terrified anybody has had an expiry date printed on it somewhere. The empires that once looked permanent enough to build a life around are now chapters in books that schoolchildren find boring. The thing pressing on you this week has a shelf life; he does not. His authority is not up for renewal at the end of history. The end of history is simply when everybody finds out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He put all things under his feet” — Paul is quoting Psalm 8:6, and every Jewish reader would catch it. That psalm was about humanity: the dignity God gave us at creation, crowned with glory and set to rule the earth. That was Adam’s commission — and it was lost. Hebrews quotes the same psalm and adds the ache: “at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him” (Heb. 2:8). Made to rule, we live instead under sin, death, and decay. “But we see him who… for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory” (Heb. 2:9). What Adam failed to hold, the Last Adam has won. The feet once nailed to a cross are now the feet beneath which every power is placed.

Their subjection is not yet fully visible, but it is already fully real — “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:25–26). We live between the decisive battle and the final surrender, and the outcome is not in doubt.

And all of it is given “to the church.” The one who rules everything rules it on behalf of his people; every force that threatens them is under the feet of their own head. Sinclair Ferguson notes that the church’s great need in every age is to see Christ as big as he actually is — we shrink him to the size of our problems and then wonder why we feel overwhelmed. Paul’s cure is not to shrink the problems but to show the immensity of the one who holds all things under his feet for us.

Stay with those last three words a little longer, because they are the strangest in the verse and we tend to hurry past them. God gave him as head over all things to the church. Not to the angels, who never fell. Not to the nations, who are vast and impressive. To the church — that is, to a scattered collection of ordinary people, many of them slaves and tradesmen, meeting in borrowed rooms in a city that would not have noticed if they vanished. The universe has been placed under one head, and that head has been handed over as a gift to them.

Which turns the whole thing round. We instinctively picture two separate stories: the big one out there — empires, markets, wars, the news — and the small one in here, our own life and our own church. This verse says there is one story, and it is being run with reference to the second. The same hand holds both. That is what Paul means elsewhere when he says all things work together for good to those who love God (Rom. 8:28); not that every event is pleasant, but that nothing is happening on a separate track, indifferent to you.

And notice which image he chooses for that authority. Not a general over an army or a magistrate over a province, but a head over a body — which in Paul carries two things at once. Authority, certainly; but also supply, for a head is the source from which the body is nourished and held together (Col. 2:19). So the sovereignty of Christ over everything is not merely the guarantee that nothing can crush you. It is the arrangement by which you are fed. The universe is being administered so that a body may be sustained.

Then the last comfort, which follows from the picture itself: a body goes where its head goes. If the head has been raised and seated above every power, the body cannot be left behind on the floor — a point Paul is about to make explicitly (2:6). So when the world seems out of control, the question is never really whether somebody is in charge. Something is always in charge. The question is whose side he is on, and this verse answers it before you can ask: he was given to you.

verseByVerse.quote: which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The fullness of him who fills all in all” — one of Paul’s most unusual phrases. Why say Christ fills all things rather than simply that he rules them? Because filling is richer than ruling. A king can hold authority over a land he has never visited; authority can be exercised from outside. But to fill something is to be present within it, to permeate it, to leave no part untouched. Paul is not describing a distant sovereign issuing decrees but a Christ whose living presence penetrates every dimension of what exists.

The language is soaked in the Old Testament. “Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the Lord” (Jer. 23:24). “If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, you are there” (Ps. 139:8). Most vividly, when Solomon dedicated the Temple, the cloud of God’s glory filled the house so completely that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11) — not overseeing it from above but filling it from within, the sign that God truly dwelt there. Paul takes that whole tradition and applies it to the risen Jesus: the one who filled the Temple now fills all things with living, transforming presence.

And then the wonder: Paul calls the church “his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” Christ fills the cosmos — and he calls the church the expression of that fullness on earth. When the church loves as he loves, something of his filling presence becomes visible in a broken world; when it gathers to worship, the one who fills all things is present in a particular, covenant way. The church is not a human society Christ endorses from a distance. It is the new Temple, made of living stones, filled with the glory that once filled Solomon’s house (cf. Col. 1:19; Eph. 3:19).

But the phrase raises a question worth facing, because a careful reader will feel it: is the church the fullness that fills Christ, or the fullness that is filled by him? The grammar allows both, and interpreters divide. Read the second way, the meaning is that Christ pours himself into his people until they are filled with all his fullness — which is precisely what Paul will pray for in so many words (3:19). That is almost certainly the main sense, and it guards something important: Christ lacks nothing. He was not incomplete before Genesis 1, and he did not acquire a missing part at Pentecost.

And yet do not tidy the sentence up too quickly, because Paul has chosen an image that deliberately leans the other way. A head without a body is not a lesser head; it is a horror. He could have said king and kingdom, or master and servants, and left himself entirely intact and separate. Instead he picked the one relationship in which the greater party looks unfinished without the lesser. He does not need us in the way we need him — but he has bound himself to us so closely that he is willing to be spoken of as incomplete until we are gathered in. That is not a deficiency in Christ. It is a measure of how far love has committed itself.

And it sets a weight on ordinary church life that most of us never feel on a Sunday. A body is simply how a person acts in the world. Your hands are how you are present to the things you pick up; your voice is how you are present to the people you speak to. Christ, who fills all things, has chosen a body through which to act visibly in this world, and it is not an institution or a building. It is the people who were in the room with you last Sunday — including the ones you find difficult. When they carry a meal to a widow, that is not merely kindness organised by volunteers; it is the fullness of the one who fills all in all, becoming visible on a particular street.

Which also means there is nowhere you can go this week that lies outside him. He fills all in all — the ward, the school run, the office where nobody prays, the flat you come home to when it is empty. You do not carry him into those places like a package. He is already filling them, and he has given you a body to belong to and a head to be joined to, so that you go in as part of him.

2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the gospel in its most concentrated and most searching form, and it opens with a diagnosis so radical it takes the breath away. We were dead. Not sick, not wounded, not spiritually impaired — dead. The Greek word is nekros, the same word used for a corpse. Paul is not being poetic; he is being precise. Before God's intervention, the human being in their natural state is spiritually lifeless — incapable of generating their own salvation, incapable of seeking God, incapable even of responding to God without God's prior action. The standard is not low; it is absolute. Dead people do not cooperate with their resurrection. They receive it.

And then — with two words that are among the most glorious in all of Scripture — the diagnosis is shattered by a declaration: But God. Rich in mercy. Because of His great love with which He loved us. Even when we were dead in our trespasses. God acted. He made us alive together with Christ. He raised us up with Him. He seated us with Him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. Three movements of sovereign grace, each one more astonishing than the last — and the purpose of all of it: "so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus." We are not saved merely for our own benefit. We are saved to be the eternal showcase of grace — the exhibit that the universe will study for ages to come, marvelling at the kindness of a God who raised the spiritually dead and made them heirs of glory.

The passage closes with one of the clearest articulations of the gospel anywhere in the Bible: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (vv.8–9). And then the stunning turn of v.10: we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works which God prepared beforehand. Salvation is not by works — but it is absolutely for works.
