Grace is not the enemy of effort; it is the only soil in which genuine, God-honouring effort can grow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

"Dead in trespasses and sins" is the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its most direct biblical expression. Total depravity does not mean that fallen human beings are as evil as they could possibly be — common grace restrains the full expression of human sin. It means that every faculty of the human person — mind, will, affections, conscience — has been corrupted by the fall, so that no part of us naturally seeks God or is capable of saving itself. The will is not neutral, waiting to choose God if only given sufficient reason; it is enslaved, "following the prince of the power of the air" (v.2), "carrying out the desires of the body and the mind" (v.3).

Against this backdrop, the "but God" of v.4 is the hinge of history. God does not respond to a seeking sinner; He acts on a dead one. This is irresistible grace — not grace that overrides the will by force, but grace that transforms the will, making the dead alive, making the unwilling willing, making the seeking possible. Calvin's comment on v.5 is unforgettable: "If we are to seek the cause of our salvation, we shall find it not in ourselves but in God alone." The new birth is entirely God's work, and the faith through which we receive it is itself His gift (v.8).

The closing verse — "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" — is the Reformed answer to the charge that grace produces passivity. It does not. Grace produces the very thing that law could only demand. The person who knows they are entirely saved by grace, not by works, is freed from self-justifying performance and freed for genuine, joyful, Spirit-empowered good works — the works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The recipients of Paul's letter knew exactly what he meant by "dead in trespasses and sins" — it was their autobiography. Many had been worshippers of Artemis, practitioners of occult arts (Acts 19:19 tells us that converted Ephesians burned their magic books, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver). The darkness, the slavery to spiritual powers, the restless seeking for blessing through ritual and charm — they had lived it. The "but God" of v.4 was the turning point of their actual lives. The grace Paul describes was not theological theory to them; it was the story of what had happened to them, written in their own experience. This is why the passage carries such heat — Paul is describing something he and his readers have lived through, not merely thought about.

Now: "Dead in trespasses and sins" describes every human being outside of Christ, however educated, however moral, however spiritually sincere. The kind CEO, the generous philanthropist, the sincere seeker of truth — apart from Christ, all share the same condition: spiritual death, living under the dominion of the one who still holds sway over "the sons of disobedience" (v.2). This is not a comfortable diagnosis, but it is a necessary one — because a person who thinks they are merely ill will never seek the cure appropriate to death. The church must have the courage to declare both the diagnosis and the remedy with equal clarity: dead — but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul opens chapter 2 with a word that lands like a stone: nekrous — dead. Not sick, not wounded, not weakened. Dead. And he means it precisely. A corpse can be dressed beautifully and look presentable; it is still a corpse. The spiritually dead person may be cultured, generous, admirable — death in Paul’s sense does not touch any of that. It means the absence of life toward God: no power to perceive him (“the natural person… is not able to understand,” 1 Cor. 2:14), no desire for him (the mind of the flesh “does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot,” Rom. 8:7–8), and no ability to change it. A weak man can try harder; a sick man can take medicine; a dead man can do neither. Lazarus did not help Jesus raise him — he heard a voice speak life into death and came out (John 11:43–44). That is what salvation is.

And notice: Paul says dead in trespasses and sins, not merely because of them. Paraptōmata (deliberate steppings-across a known line) and hamartia (missing the mark) are not an external punishment that caused the death; they are the death itself. To live in them is already to be in the realm of death, cut off from the source of life. Which is why the cure cannot be moral improvement. You do not improve a corpse. You raise it.

And death, in Paul’s picture, is not static — it walks. “In which you once walked”: the dead are not lying still. They are moving, following, going somewhere — and Paul names the two currents that carried them. The first is “the course of this world.” The word is aiōn, the age — not the planet, which God made and loves, but the whole running of human society organised as though God were not there. It is a current, and the dead do not feel it, because nothing feels less like being swept along than swimming with the tide. You discover the current only when you turn and try to swim against it. The second is personal: “the prince of the power of the air.” That is Satan — a real person, not a figure of speech for society’s bad habits — ruling a real dominion; Paul will name his forces plainly enough later (6:12). “The air” is the realm between heaven and earth, the ancient way of saying: near, pervasive, atmospheric — the pressure you breathe without ever noticing it is there. So with the flesh of verse 3, the three great enemies stand together in a single sentence: the world around, the devil above, the flesh within. And mark what the dead man is doing about them. He is not fighting them. He is following them. That is what makes the diagnosis so grave — he is not a prisoner straining at the bars but a corpse carried by the tide (cf. 1 John 2:15–16; John 8:44).

R.C. Sproul used to say that total depravity is the most universally rejected and the most urgently needed truth in the Christian message — not because it demeans us but because it tells the truth. A doctor who softens a fatal diagnosis to spare feelings is not kind but negligent. And Paul’s diagnosis is not the sentence; it is the setup. The word “dead” exists to make verse 5 blaze: “even when we were dead… he made us alive.” The depth of the death is the measure of the miracle (cf. Col. 2:13; Ezek. 37:1–14).

One objection needs answering here, because almost everybody feels it and few people say it out loud: dead? I know unbelievers who are kinder, steadier and more generous than half the congregation. How can that be a corpse?

Think of cut flowers. A florist’s arrangement can be lovelier than anything still growing in the garden — brighter, better shaped, more fragrant in the room. Nobody looking at it would say it is dead. And yet it has been severed from its root, and everything you admire about it is running on borrowed time. It is not less beautiful than the rooted plant. It is simply no longer connected to what keeps it alive. That is Paul’s point exactly. He is not claiming that unbelievers behave worse than believers, which would be plainly false and would insult people we know and love. He is saying something about connection, not comparison: cut off from God, however admirably a life is arranged, it has no life toward him — no perception of him, no desire for him, and no power to reconnect itself. The kindness is real. The beauty is real. The root is what is missing.

And that gives you a test you can actually run, which does not depend on how you feel today. Corpses do not develop appetites. So if you find in yourself any hunger for God at all — if you would rather be near him than not, if his word occasionally lands with weight, if sin now grieves you where once it barely registered — then something has already happened to you that you did not do. You are not looking at evidence of your strength. You are looking at evidence that a voice has spoken into a grave, and that you heard it.

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“We all,” Paul says — Jew and Gentile alike, no one exempt. And he traces the ruin to its root: “the passions of our flesh.” Sarx (“flesh”) does not mean the physical body — God made the body good, the Son took it on, the resurrection is bodily. It means fallen human nature, the whole person, body and mind, curved in on itself — Augustine’s incurvatus in se. So the passions of the flesh are not merely sexual; Galatians 5 lists idolatry, jealousy, rivalry, and fits of anger alongside immorality. The flesh produces boardroom sin as readily as bedroom sin. The respectable man who has never been immoral but lives for status and control is operating in the flesh as fully as anyone.

Paul adds “the desires of body and mind,” closing the moralist’s last escape. Discipline your appetites and you may simply have moved the problem upstairs — to intellectual pride, the lust for power, the craving to be admired. Jesus said as much: the man who never touched adultery but nursed it in his heart is not standing on clean ground (Matt. 5:28). The whole person is implicated.

“By nature children of wrath.” That little word phusei — “by nature” — is original sin in a phrase. The fallenness is not an add-on to an otherwise neutral self; it goes all the way down. We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners. And “wrath” is not God losing his temper. It is the settled, holy opposition of a righteous God to everything evil. As Sproul put it, if God were not wrathful toward sin he would not be good — a judge who feels nothing when the guilty walk free is not merciful but corrupt (cf. Rom. 1:18). To be “children of wrath” is to have a nature that justly stands under that judgment.

This is not cruelty; it is the only foundation on which real gratitude can be built. Tim Keller often noted that the one forgiven little loves little. The shallowness of our worship usually matches the smallness of our sense of what we were saved from. When you know what you were, you know what grace is — and the “but God” of the next verse lands with all its weight (cf. Rom. 5:8–10).

Two things should be added, because this verse frightens people, and not always in the way it is meant to.

The first is a question anyone raised on fairness will ask: how can I be held responsible for a nature I was born with and never chose? Leave the theology aside for a moment and simply observe. Nobody has ever had to teach a child to lie, or to grab, or to say mine. We teach the opposite, constantly, at enormous effort, and with mixed results. Every parent is an unwilling expert witness on original sin. And the doctrine has never been that you are punished as an outsider for somebody else’s crime; it is that you were born into a family and have signed its charter with your own hand every day since. Paul is not describing an injustice done to you. He is describing something you would recognise in yourself if you were honest for ten minutes.

The second is the tense, and it is the whole comfort of the paragraph. Read the verb again: we were by nature children of wrath. Not are. Every dreadful word in these three verses stands in the past tense — dead, walked, followed, lived, were — and they are all held there, waiting, until two words in verse 4 break over them: But God. So if you are in Christ, this passage is not your diagnosis. It is your medical history. It is the thing you are reading about, not the thing you are living in. Read it as a Christian ought to read it — not with dread, wondering whether it still describes you, but the way a healthy man reads an old chart from the worst year of his life, and marvels that he is sitting up and reading anything at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But God.” Two words — the pivot of the passage, of redemptive history, of every Christian life. Martyn Lloyd-Jones said they may be the two most important words in the Bible. You were dead — but God. A child of wrath — but God. Without hope — but God. Every testimony, however complex, reduces to this hinge.

He is “rich in mercy” — plousios, the language of wealth and overflow. Not adequate mercy, not mercy that barely covers the debt, but mercy that does not run low or grow harder to obtain the more you have needed it. Mercy and grace are close but distinct, and Paul uses both here: grace gives what we do not deserve; mercy withholds what we do. Mercy looks at misery and moves toward it. The Hebrew behind it is hesed — loyal covenant love — and the Greek eleos is active compassion. Mercy sees the corpse and is not repelled; it does not wait for signs of improvement before it acts. It moves first.

And it had to be rich, because the debt was total. A man forgiven a hundred pounds is grateful; a man forgiven an unpayable, infinite debt has no words. Jesus told that parable exactly: the one forgiven much loves much (Luke 7:41–43). Paul wants you to feel the full weight of “rich,” so that the love it produces is equally rich.

And under it all is love — “the great love with which he loved us.” God did not act from duty. He looked at the spiritually dead, the children of wrath, and loved them — not what they would become, but what they actually were — and moved toward them anyway (cf. Rom. 5:8; Titus 3:5; Lam. 3:22–23).

And now the verb, which is the thing God actually did and the point this whole sentence has been travelling toward. He made us alive. Not helped. Not improved. Not offered a second chance to make better use of the first. Paul has spent three verses establishing that we were corpses precisely so that this word would have nothing to compete with, because there is exactly one thing you can do for a dead man. You cannot offer him advice, or terms, or an opportunity, or an incentive. You can raise him. That is the entire list, and it is what Paul says God did.

Notice as well the sort of word he builds in order to say it: synezōopoiēsen — made alive together with. That little prefix, syn-, is about to be repeated twice in the very next verse: raised with him, seated with him. Paul is not describing three separate miracles that happen to resemble what occurred to Christ. He is saying your life is not a parallel resurrection of your own but a share in his. When Jesus came out of that tomb, you came out with him. Your resurrection is not pending approval somewhere; in him it is already historical, and it happened outside Jerusalem long before you were born.

And hold on to the timing, because Paul is careful with it: even when we were dead. Not once we had begun to stir. Not after a decent interval of moral effort had shown some promise. At the precise moment when there was least to work with and nothing whatever to reward — that is when he acted. Which quietly settles the question every anxious believer comes back to sooner or later, whether God might yet think better of it and change his mind about him. You contributed nothing at all to your first resurrection. Your standing has never once rested on your contribution, and it is not about to start now.

So read the sentence through one more time and let its shape do the work. The subject is God. The verb is made alive. And the object — the thing acted upon, contributing nothing, entirely passive from beginning to end — is you.

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verbs, each built on the prefix sun- (“with”): made alive with him, raised with him, seated with him. Not three events but one reality seen from three angles — what happened to Christ at his resurrection and ascension happened to the believer by union with him. The fate of the head determines the fate of the body.

And the most astonishing is stated not as a hope but as accomplished fact: you are seated “in the heavenly places” — the verb is past tense, completed. The heavenly places are not a spot above the clouds but the realm of ultimate spiritual reality, where Christ is enthroned above every power (1:20) and where the decisive matters of existence are settled. How can someone still walking the earth be seated there? Union with Christ. When God raised and seated his Son, he did it not for Christ alone but as the head of a body. So you are, at this moment, both walking around in a weak and mortal body and seated with Christ in God’s sight. The earthly experience is what you feel; the heavenly position is what God sees — and both are equally real (Col. 3:1–3).

To be “seated” is the posture of finished work and settled authority. Old Testament priests never sat in the Temple; their work was never done. But Christ “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” because his one sacrifice was final (Heb. 1:3) — and you are seated with him, sharing his rest and security, not by anything you earned but simply because you are in him.

This is already true, though not yet fully experienced — the “already” and the “not yet” run side by side through the whole Christian life. But the position is real now. So when anxiety says everything is out of control, the answer is not to deny the chaos but to remember where you sit — with the one who has all things under his feet. When the accuser says you are disqualified, do not produce your record; point to your location: I am in the one who sits above every power. The heavenly seat is not a feeling to generate but a fact to believe — and believed deeply, it reshapes everything.

There is one detail in that phrase which is easy to miss and worth a great deal once seen. “The heavenly places” is an expression peculiar to this letter, and Paul uses it five times. Watch where it keeps turning up. It is where Christ is enthroned above every power (1:20). It is where you have been seated (2:6). It is where the church displays the manifold wisdom of God to watching powers (3:10). And it is where the spiritual forces of evil operate, and where our real struggle is fought (6:12).

So the realm you have been seated in is the very realm where the war is going on. That is what saves this verse from becoming escapism, which is the standing danger in any talk of a heavenly seat. Paul is not offering you a quiet room above the noise. He is telling you your position within the conflict: not safely away from it, but above it, seated with the one against whom none of those powers can move. It is the difference between a soldier pinned down in a trench, who cannot see the field and does not know whether his side is winning, and a man standing beside the commander with the whole battle laid out in front of him. Both are in the war. Only one of them knows how it ends.

And notice, finally, that nothing here is graded. Paul does not say that the mature are seated while the struggling stand at the back. There is no seniority in this seat. The believer converted last Thursday, who still cannot find Habakkuk and is fighting something he has not yet told anybody about, is seated exactly where the apostle is seated — because neither of them is there on his own account. They are both there in Christ, and he is only seated once.

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul lifts his eyes from the miracle of salvation to its ultimate horizon. God saved his people not merely to rescue them from wrath — though that alone would be more than enough — but “so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us.” The audience and the timescale are staggering.

“The coming ages” is plural — not a single static moment but an unfolding eternity with depth we cannot yet imagine. Paul does not over-specify, and neither should we; but the direction is clear. What we have tasted here — forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, God’s presence in prayer — is the down payment. The coming ages are the feast. And three words strain to describe it: the grace is immeasurable (beyond every category), its supply is riches (inexhaustible), and it comes in kindness — a tender, personal word, God face to face delighting to give his people more of himself forever.

We cannot picture the scale, and that is the point. But reach for the direction: think of your most profound moment of grace — when forgiveness felt most real, when a promise landed and you could barely breathe. That came through a fallen mind, a weak faith, a tired body, in a world still cursed. What will it be when every barrier is gone? What you have tasted is real — a single drop from an ocean that has no shore. C.S. Lewis caught it at the end of The Last Battle: every room opens into a still greater one, “further up and further in,” and the cry is, “this is the land I have been looking for all my life.”

And the display is not only for our enjoyment but for God’s glory. Every saved sinner is an exhibit of grace, proof across all eternity that God is exactly who he claimed to be. Even now the angels and powers are watching what God does with sinners (3:10). What they will see, forever, is the immeasurable kindness of a God who took the undeserving, seated them with his Son, and gave them everything (cf. 1 Cor. 2:9; Rev. 21:3–4).

But do not slide past who the exhibit actually is. God is mounting a display that will run through the coming ages, and the items on show are not galaxies or landscapes; he has those already, and they never cost him anything. What will be exhibited, for ever, is what he did with people. You are the exhibit.

Which turns something painful inside out. Most of us carry a chapter we would rather were left out of the account — the years we wasted, the thing we still cannot say out loud, the person we were before. We quietly assume that heaven will involve a discreet silence about all that. But look again at what is being displayed: not your record, but the immeasurable riches of his grace. And grace can only be measured against what it had to overcome. A restorer’s skill is never demonstrated by a painting that was never damaged. The deeper the ruin, the greater the display — which means the very chapter you would erase is the part of you that will testify most loudly, and for ever, to what he is like. In the coming ages nobody will be embarrassed by your past. They will be looking at it and worshipping.

And kindness is the word he chooses for the manner of it — chrēstotēs, warm and personal, the kindness of someone leaning toward you rather than a benefactor signing a cheque at a distance. Eternity is not God finally getting round to a reward you were owed. It is God, for ever, delighting to be kind to people who had nothing whatever coming.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” — the whole of it, faith included. Faith is not a human contribution that triggers grace; it is the empty hand that receives it, and the entire transaction is God’s gift. John MacArthur presses the logic: if even one element of salvation depended on us, the final difference between the saved and the lost would trace back to something in us — and Paul will not allow that.

A careful reader with a study Bible will meet an objection here, and it deserves a straight answer. The Greek word for “this” (touto) is neuter, while the word for “faith” (pistis) is feminine — they do not grammatically agree, so, the note will say, “this” cannot refer to faith; it points back to the whole preceding statement — salvation by grace through faith — and calls that the gift. Grant the grammar entirely. It does not weaken the doctrine; it strengthens it. For if “this” sweeps back over the whole of what Paul has just said, then grace, salvation, and the faith by which it is received are all gathered into the single word gift. You do not rescue a place for human contribution by narrowing the pronoun; the neuter takes in everything and hands it all to God. And even on the narrower reading, faith is called a gift plainly enough elsewhere: “it has been granted to you… to believe” (Phil. 1:29); the Corinthians “believed through grace” (Acts 18:27); their faith was something “obtained” (2 Pet. 1:1). The doctrine does not hang on one disputed pronoun. Wherever you draw the line, nothing survives that a saved sinner could boast in — which is exactly Paul’s next point.

“So that no one may boast.” The ancient world ran on honour; boasting was not just a personality flaw but a social institution, and the only question was in what you boasted. Paul had a résumé to stand on — circumcised the eighth day, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless under the law (Phil. 3:4–6) — and he called all of it skybalon, rubbish, next to knowing Christ. For if salvation held any human contribution — a wiser decision, a moral effort that tipped the scales — the saved could say, “I am in and you are out, and the difference, at some level, is me.” That is boasting, and grace rules it out completely (cf. 1 Cor. 1:29–31).

We rarely beat our chests about it, but the boasting takes subtler forms: the quiet sense that I believed because I was wiser or more open than those who did not; the Calvinist grateful for election who privately feels more perceptive than others; the seasoned member eyeing the new convert with a touch of seniority; the comparing of spiritual histories, as though the one saved young has cleaner standing than the one saved at seventy. Both came to the cross with nothing; both left with the same righteousness of Christ. Even the testimony can quietly cast the speaker as the hero who finally worked it out — when the properly told story does the opposite: the more undeserving the sinner, the more brilliant the grace. John Newton knew which way the glory flowed — “that saved a wretch like me” (cf. 1 Cor. 1:27–31; Gal. 6:14).

Two things remain, and both are for the reader who is not arguing about grace at all but quietly worrying about himself.

The first is the tense, which in Greek carries more than the English easily shows. Paul does not write that you are being saved, nor that you may yet be saved if things hold together to the end. He uses a perfect: you have been saved — an action completed, with a result that goes on standing. And he casts it in the passive, so that the one who performed it is not you. Something was done to you; it was finished; and its effect continues into the room you are sitting in now. Which is also why assurance is not arrogance. The man who says he is saved is no more boasting about his performance than a rescued swimmer boasts about the lifeboat. He is simply reporting a completed action carried out by somebody else.

The second is for anyone who has read this paragraph and thought: yes, but is my faith the right sort? Mine feels so thin. Notice that Paul never once praises the faith itself. He does not call it strong, or sincere, or sufficient. He calls it the channel — saved through faith — and its entire value lies in what it lays hold of. Weak faith in a sound bridge will carry you over the river; robust faith in a rotten one will drop you into it. The bridge does the saving, not the confidence with which you stepped onto it. Which is why the Lord could speak of faith the size of a mustard seed, and why the father who cried “I believe; help my unbelief!” went home with a healed son (Mark 9:24). Nobody in Scripture is ever saved by the excellence of his believing.

So the question to ask is never whether your faith is big enough. That question turns you back on yourself, and the honest answer to it will always be no. The question is what you are trusting. Put a trembling hand on Christ and you have all that he is; and the empty hand, which is all faith ever was, does not become any emptier for shaking.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Workmanship” is poiēma — the word behind “poem.” You are God’s work of art, his masterpiece; the God who spoke the cosmos into being has spoken new creation into you. And that identity is the ground of everything else in the verse.

Having insisted for two verses that salvation is not by works, Paul now brings works back — carefully. They are not the root of salvation but its fruit; not the foundation but the outcome. And he gives no checklist, deliberately: good works are the whole range of faithful, loving, God-directed life that flows from a heart made new — mercy to the poor and the stranger (James 1:27; Matt. 25:35–36), integrity in ordinary things (honest work, a faithful marriage, patience with hard people — the very things he lists in 4:25–32), and witness to Christ (1 Pet. 3:15). The plumber who works well and charges fairly, the employee who works as to the Lord (6:7), the parent who disciplines with warmth (6:4) — these are good works in Paul’s sense.

And they are “prepared beforehand” — God laid them out before you existed. Not that you are a robot running a script, but that the life of good works is not something you must invent from scratch or sustain by willpower. God has already woven a path through the terrain of your particular life and gifts. As Thomas Watson said, God not only prepares us for good works, he prepares good works for us. So the question is not “what good works should I invent?” but “what has God placed in front of me?” — the neighbour in need, the unexpected chance to serve, the gift waiting to be used.

None of this is the basis of your acceptance — verses 8–9 shut that door. A child does not obey to earn a place in the family; he obeys because he already belongs. But neither are the works optional: you were created for them, and a faith that bears no fruit is not living faith (James 2:17; Matt. 7:17). Nor are they only the dramatic gestures — a mission trip, a large gift. They are listening well to the lonely, returning to apologise, doing a hidden job thoroughly. We are God’s masterpiece — and masterpieces are made not to be stored but displayed (cf. Matt. 5:16; Titus 2:14).

Two details in the wording repay a second look, and then a word for the reader who has just read “masterpiece” and thought: not me.

The first is that poiēma appears only twice in the whole New Testament. Here — and in Romans 1:20, where it means the created universe, the things that have been made, through which God’s power and divine nature are plainly seen. So the word Paul reaches for to describe the galaxies is the word he reaches for to describe you. And of those two works, the second cost him far more. The first he spoke into being; the second required a death.

The second detail is a word he has already used in this very chapter, and it slips past because it is so ordinary: walk. Back in verse 2 that is precisely what the dead were doing — “in which you once walked, following the course of this world.” Now, at the close of the same paragraph: “that we should walk in them.” The same verb, the opposite road. And notice he does not say we should admire the good works, or intend them, or feel warmly disposed toward them. Walk. It is the plainest and least dramatic word available, and it is chosen: a walk is made of steps, and steps are taken one at a time, in a particular direction, usually with nobody watching. The old life was a walk as well. Conversion did not stop you walking. It changed the road.

And now for the reader who cannot make the word masterpiece fit what he sees in the mirror. Notice first that you are not the one being asked to assess the work. You are standing inside it while it is still being made, which is the one vantage point from which no work of art has ever looked finished. A house halfway through renovation looks considerably worse than it did before anybody touched it — walls opened up, floors lifted, dust over everything — and that is not evidence that the builder has failed. It is evidence that he has begun. What you are looking at is not the finished piece. And the worth of a work is set by the artist, never by the material’s opinion of itself; the marble does not get a vote. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Phil. 1:6) — and he does not abandon canvases.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If vv.1–10 describe the miracle of individual salvation, vv.11–22 describe its corporate consequence — and the consequence is nothing less than the creation of a new humanity. The most profound social division of the ancient world was the division between Jew and Gentile. It was not merely ethnic; it was religious, covenantal, cultic, and moral. The Jew had the oracles of God, the covenants of promise, the temple, the law, the Messiah. The Gentile was "separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world" (v.12). The wall between them was literal — the Jerusalem temple had a stone barrier (the soreg) beyond which Gentiles could not pass on pain of death. And spiritually, the distance was infinite.

Christ has abolished it. Not by lowering the standard, not by relativising the covenant, not by pretending the distinction never mattered — but by fulfilling what the distinction pointed to and then, in His own body on the cross, "killing the hostility" (v.16). He made peace. Not peace by negotiation, not peace by compromise, but peace by blood — His own blood, shed for both Jew and Gentile, making one new man in place of two. The dividing wall of hostility has been broken down in Christ. The sign above the gate that once said "Keep Out" has been torn down and replaced with a welcome: "You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ" (v.13).

The result is a building — a temple. Not the old temple in Jerusalem, with its courts of separation and its stone barrier. A new temple, built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. The church is God's dwelling place by the Spirit. What the Jerusalem temple was in shadow, the church now is in reality: the place where God lives, the community through which He makes Himself known to the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

This passage reveals the ecclesiological dimensions of the atonement — a dimension often underemphasised in evangelical theology. We tend to think of Christ's death in purely individual terms: He died for me, my sins are forgiven, I am reconciled to God. All of this is gloriously true. But Paul insists that the cross accomplished something more: it created a new community. Christ died not only to reconcile individuals to God (vertical reconciliation) but to reconcile estranged human beings to one another (horizontal reconciliation). He "reconciled us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (v.16).

This means that the unity of the church is not merely a practical or organisational goal; it is a theological reality purchased by Christ's blood. To live in division, to maintain the walls that Christ has torn down, to prefer the company of people like us over the diverse community Christ has created — this is a denial of the atonement. Every genuinely reconciled, cross-cultural Christian community is a proclamation of the gospel: not with words but with existence. Its very existence says: the cross is real, the wall is down, God has made one new man.

The metaphor of the temple (vv.19–22) carries the further implication that the church's holiness matters. The old temple was the place where God dwelt, and its holiness was fiercely guarded. The new temple — the church — is also the dwelling place of God by His Spirit. The community of believers is not merely a gathering of like-minded people; it is the sacred space where the Holy God has chosen to make His home on earth. This gives both dignity and responsibility to every local church: you are the temple of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The stone wall of the Jerusalem temple — the soreg — was not a metaphor. Inscriptions warning Gentiles that entry beyond it meant death have been found by archaeologists. The barrier was physical, legal, and deadly. When Paul says Christ has broken down "the dividing wall of hostility," his Jewish and Gentile readers understood exactly what wall he meant. They may have stood on opposite sides of it. Now they sat side by side at the Lord's table, eating and drinking together, addressed as fellow citizens and members of the same household. The sociological miracle was visible and daily, and it pointed to a theological reality: the cross had accomplished what no social programme could.

Now: The church in our age still struggles with the walls that Christ has torn down. Racial segregation in churches persists in many places. Class divisions shape congregational culture in ways we rarely examine. Political tribalism has entered sanctuaries and split families of faith. Against all of this, Ephesians 2 speaks with prophetic force: the wall is down. Christ killed the hostility. The new humanity He created is more fundamental than any human division that preceded it. The church that reflects this — that is visibly, sacrificially, joyfully diverse across the lines that divide the surrounding world — is not merely being socially progressive. It is being theologically faithful. It is showing the world what the cross actually accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pauses to command: remember. Before he describes the miracle of vv.13–22, he wants his Gentile readers to feel the boundary they were once outside — the sharpest religious line in the ancient world. They were “Gentiles in the flesh,” outside the covenant story God had been telling through Israel, and they were called “the uncircumcision” by their Jewish neighbours — not a neutral word but a stigma, a reminder of their exclusion every time it arose (recall the contempt in David’s “this uncircumcised Philistine,” 1 Sam. 17:26).

Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham, the mark of belonging to God’s people (Gen. 17). But Paul adds a pointed qualifier — it was “made in the flesh by hands.” He does not despise it; it had real value as a sign (Rom. 3:1–2). But he is preparing his argument: the physical mark made by human hands is no longer the boundary that defines who is in. The new-covenant reality is circumcision of the heart, given by the Spirit, not achieved by the flesh (Rom. 2:28–29; Col. 2:11). He starts here because the wider the chasm looks, the more astonishing the bridge becomes.

Notice that remembering has to be commanded. Paul does not suggest it or recommend it; he issues it as an order, because forgetting is what we do naturally, and Christians forget this particular thing faster than most. The believer of thirty years, or the one raised in a Christian home who cannot recall a time before, drifts imperceptibly toward feeling like the sort of person God would naturally have wanted — as though grace had found something in him worth finding. The cure for that is not a mood. It is an act of deliberate recollection, performed on purpose, of what you were and where you once stood.

God had trained Israel in exactly this discipline. Again and again the law tells them to remember that they were slaves in Egypt — and never as a bare historical note. It is nearly always attached to a command about somebody else: remember you were a slave, therefore release your servant generously (Deut. 15:15); you know the heart of a stranger, therefore do not oppress the foreigner (Exod. 23:9). Memory of your own rescue was meant to become the engine of your treatment of outsiders. Paul is doing the identical thing here. He is about to tell a mixed and uneasy church to live as one body, and he begins by reminding the Gentile half precisely how far outside they themselves once stood.

And look again at the name they were given: the uncircumcision. It is not a description of anything they were. It defines a whole people by an absence — by the mark they did not carry. Every community has words like that, and they all work the same way: they reduce a human being to a lack. Paul quotes it on purpose, letting his readers hear once more the word that used to put them outside, so that they will never be comfortable using its equivalent about anybody else. A man who genuinely remembers being on the outside cannot easily keep another person there.

verseByVerse.quote: remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul lines up five descriptions of Gentile existence before Christ, each deeper than the last — the fullest portrait of human lostness in the New Testament. Not to shame the reader, but so that the rescue in v.13 lands with full weight: you cannot treasure the nearness without first feeling the distance.

First, separated from Christ — the foundational deprivation from which the rest flow. Israel lived in the orbit of the coming Messiah, prepared by promise and prophet; the Gentile world had none of it, no framework in which his coming could even be expected. Second, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel — shut out from the community through which God was visibly at work in history, able to watch the story from outside but with no share in it. Third, strangers to the covenants of promise — a xenos, an alien with no standing in the household, no claim on what God had bound himself to give: the seed who would bless the nations (Gen. 12:3), the everlasting throne (2 Sam. 7:12–13), the new covenant on the heart (Jer. 31:31–34).

Fourth, having no hope — not merely a gloomy mood but no basis for hope. The ancient world was full of religion, temples on every corner; what it lacked was any certain promise that death was not the end. Its own tombstones tell the story: “I was not; I was; I am not; I care not.” Fifth, and darkest, without God — atheoi, godless. Not that they denied all deity; they worshipped constantly. But they lacked the one true God who had revealed himself by name and kept his promises. Surrounded by gods, they were, in the most precise sense, without God.

And Paul says: remember this — not to reopen shame but to calibrate gratitude. You cannot fully receive a rescue you have forgotten you needed. Five darknesses — and then a single light in v.13 that makes all five vanish: “but now in Christ Jesus” (cf. 1 Cor. 8:4–5).

Read that list once more with a particular reader in view, because Paul has assembled the exact vocabulary of exclusion. Alienated. Strangers. No hope. Without God. If you have ever stood at the edge of a group and known, without anyone having to say it, that you did not belong — the family you married into, the workplace where the others share a history you do not, even the church where everybody else appears to have known each other for years — then you already know the flavour of every word in this sentence. Paul is not writing in the abstract. He is naming one of the most painful experiences a human being can have, and telling you that it was once your actual standing before God, in the only place where belonging finally counts.

Which is why what follows is aimed exactly where it hurts. He does not say that the outsiders were given advice, or a procedure by which they might work their way in over time, or a probationary period. He says they were brought near — by somebody else’s blood, and in a single movement. And notice what that does to the five items on the list. They are not softened or improved. They are reversed, one by one: no longer separated from Christ but in him; no longer alienated but citizens; no longer strangers to the covenants but heirs of them; no longer without hope but holding an inheritance kept in heaven; no longer without God but indwelt by his Spirit. The whole catalogue of exclusion is answered item for item, and the answer is not a policy. It is a Person.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now” — the second great pivot of chapter 2 (the first was “but God” in v. 4). Far off / brought near is the language of Isaiah 57:19, which Paul will quote in v. 17. The distance has been closed, and the means is specific: blood. Not dialogue, not mutual understanding, not the passage of time, not a shared commitment to common values — blood.

Both halves of that sentence repay unpacking, because Paul is using vocabulary his readers would have recognised at once.

“Far off” was not a mood; it was very nearly a technical term. Jewish writers used it as shorthand for the Gentile world, and its opposite — being “brought near” — was the language used of a proselyte, someone at last admitted into the covenant people. Isaiah had promised “peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isa. 57:19), and Peter would preach that the promise is for “all who are far off” (Acts 2:39). So Paul takes the standard word for Gentile distance and answers it with the standard word for admission — and then, in the verses immediately following, blows the standard meaning apart. For how near is near? Not near enough to observe from a respectful distance. Not admitted to an outer court and told to be grateful. Within nine verses these same people are fellow citizens, then members of the household, and finally stones built into the temple where God himself lives. They began outside a barrier that threatened death to anyone who crossed it, and they end up being the building.

Then the means, and why it had to be blood. The distance was never really geographical or cultural; it was moral. Which is exactly why none of the alternatives Paul dismisses could ever have worked: dialogue does not remove guilt, the passing of time does not erase it, and a shared commitment to common values does not answer for what has actually been done. Under the law it was blood that dealt with sin, because “the life of the flesh is in the blood”, and God had given it “to make atonement” (Lev. 17:11) — a life laid down in the place of the life that had been forfeited.

And notice that this was never a Gentile problem. The Jew inside the barrier could not walk into the presence of God either. He watched a priest go in on his behalf, once a year, and never without blood (Heb. 9:7). The wall kept Gentiles out of the court; sin kept everybody out of the holiest place. So blood is not the outsider’s unfortunate entry fee, charged to latecomers. It is, and always was, the only door there has ever been — and what changed at the cross is not that a second door was opened for a second class of people, but that the true and final sacrifice was offered once, and both classes walked through it together.

One thing to hold on to when your own heart turns accuser. The nearness described here was not produced by your feeling close to God, and it is not undone by your feeling far from him. It was established by an event outside you, at a cost you did not pay and could not have raised. A believer may feel a very long way off on a Tuesday afternoon and still be, in the only sense this verse is using the word, near.

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 14 is one of the most compressed, explosive sentences in the letter, and it begins with a stress: “He himself is our peace” — autos, placed first. Not his teaching, not his example. He himself. Christ does not broker a settlement between two parties and step back; he is the peace, and it cannot be separated from his person. This matters in practice, for biblical peace is not the absence of conflict but shalom — wholeness, everything rightly related: peace with God, peace between peoples, the inner coherence of a life aimed at its true end. All of it is found in him and nowhere else. “Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27): the world manages conflict; Christ gives himself.

“Who has made us both one” — Jew and Gentile, the two great divisions of the ancient world, separated by the most entrenched boundary it knew. Not brought closer; made one, a single new humanity. The mechanism is union with Christ: two people each joined to him are thereby joined to each other, whatever their cultures say, for the ground at the foot of the cross is perfectly level (Gal. 3:28).

“And has broken down the dividing wall of hostility” — almost certainly the soreg, the stone barrier in the Jerusalem Temple that fenced Gentiles out of the inner courts. Archaeologists have recovered its inscription, warning in Greek and Latin that any Gentile who crossed did so on pain of death — and the Romans let the Jewish authorities carry it out. That wall said, in stone and law: the presence of God is not for you; stay outside. Paul says Christ demolished it — not lowered it or made it easier to cross, but broke it down. The Temple veil tearing top to bottom made the same point in the same season (Matt. 27:51): the way is open.

And it happened “in his flesh.” The wall was not dismantled by a transaction conducted at a safe distance but in the body of Jesus, on a Roman cross, on a particular Friday. The peace is not an idea and the unity is not an aspiration; the one who hung there took both hostilities — between God and man, between Jew and Gentile — into himself and did not pass them on (Col. 1:20–22).

One question presses here and deserves an answer, because any thoughtful reader will feel it. If the separation between Jew and Gentile was in some real sense God’s own doing — the law, the covenant signs, the whole apparatus of holy distinction — then how can Christ be praised for demolishing it? Is the Son undoing the Father’s work?

No. He is finishing it. The separation was never an end in itself; it was more like a cast on a broken limb. Its purpose was to preserve a particular people through whom the Messiah would come, and to teach the world over centuries, in terms nobody could mistake, that God is holy and that access to him is not a casual matter. Paul says precisely this elsewhere: the law was a guardian until Christ came (Gal. 3:23–25). And when the bone has knitted, the cast comes off — not because it was a mistake, but because it has done its work. Nobody accuses the surgeon of breaking the arm when he cuts it away.

Notice too that this unity was not a pious sentiment. It was expensive, and it did not happen by itself. For a Jewish believer it meant sitting at a table with a Gentile and eating what was on it — setting aside food laws that his forebears had been tortured and killed for refusing to break. For a Gentile it meant accepting that the salvation he now enjoyed had come through a nation he had been raised to think peculiar. Much of the book of Acts is the story of how hard this proved: a sheet let down from heaven three times before Peter would believe it (Acts 10), a council convened because the argument would not settle (Acts 15), and Peter himself later withdrawing from Gentile tables until Paul opposed him to his face (Gal. 2:11–14). Paul is not describing something that came naturally to anyone. He is announcing an accomplished fact, and then spending the rest of the letter urging the church to go and live inside it.

Which is why the verse still has work to do. The soreg is rubble; the instinct that built it is not. Every congregation has its own quiet inscriptions, and they are almost never written down: the professional and the unemployed, the settled family and the single man, the politically confident and the politically suspect, the respectable and the one whose past everybody happens to know. You can usually locate your own wall with two questions. Who do you find yourself sitting near on a Sunday without ever having decided to? And whose home have you actually been inside? Christ did not lower these barriers or make them easier to cross. He broke them down in his flesh — and a church that rebuilds them is quietly reassembling the very thing he died to destroy.

verseByVerse.quote: by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ broke the wall down “by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances” — a phrase misread in two opposite directions. Paul means the ceremonial and boundary-marking code that defined Jewish identity and kept the two peoples structurally apart: circumcision, dietary laws, purity rules, festivals, the Temple system. God gave these for a season — to keep his people distinct and to foreshadow Christ — but they were always temporary, a wall built to come down when the reality arrived. “These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Col. 2:16–17). When Christ came, the scaffolding was removed so the building could be seen.

He does not mean the moral law is abolished — the most common misreading. Jesus said plainly, “I have not come to abolish… but to fulfil” (Matt. 5:17); the moral law reflects God’s own character and stands. (Reformed theology has long distinguished the moral law, permanent; the civil, given to Israel as a nation; and the ceremonial, pointing to Christ — and it is the latter two Paul has in view.) Nor does he mean Israel’s history was a mistake: “the law was our guardian until Christ came” (Gal. 3:24), and a guardian is not an enemy. What ended was not the standard but the wall — the claim that these practices marked who was in and who was out.

And the purpose of the abolishing is creation: “that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two.” Not Gentiles absorbed into Judaism, nor Jewish identity diluted — a third thing, one new humanity that never existed before, defined not by ethnicity or law but wholly by union with Christ. The church is not a reformed synagogue with the door left open. It is a new creation, the firstfruits of the renewed humanity God has always been moving toward (cf. Gal. 3:24–28; Rom. 10:4).

Notice the verb he chooses: create. Paul does not say Christ negotiated one new man, or organised one, or assembled one from the parts available. Ktizō is creation language, the word used of what God did in Genesis, and the same word Paul used five verses ago about you personally (v. 10). Which means the church is not at bottom an institution. Anyone can found an institution; committees do it every week. Nobody can found a creature. The unity of the church is not an achievement that a sufficiently gifted leadership might reproduce somewhere else with the right method; it is something God made, and the most any of us can do is decline to damage it.

And be clear what “one new man” does not mean, because it gets misread in both directions. It does not mean a Jew stops being a Jew, or a Gentile stops being a Gentile. Paul tells converts to remain as they were called — the circumcised is not to undo it, the uncircumcised is not to seek it (1 Cor. 7:18–20). And the last picture Scripture gives us of the redeemed is not a uniform crowd in matching clothes but a great multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Rev. 7:9) — the differences are still there in glory. So this is neither a melting pot that boils the cultures away, nor a federation of groups keeping a courteous distance from one another. It is one new humanity in which the differences remain and simply stop deciding anything. Your background is still yours. It is no longer your standing.

Then the last three words, which carry more than they look: so making peace. Peace here is not a mood that eventually settled over the situation, and it is not what happens when two parties grow tired of the argument. It is a manufactured thing. Paul uses a verb of production: peace had to be made, the way anything is made — with materials, labour and cost. The material was his flesh; the labour was a crucifixion; the cost was everything he had. Which is why peace in a church is never simply the absence of friction, and never merely good manners in the porch afterwards. It is the keeping of something expensive that somebody else paid for. And that is exactly how Paul will put it two chapters later: be eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (4:3). He does not tell them to create it. It has already been created. He tells them not to lose it.

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reconciliation is first vertical (to God) and then horizontal (Jew and Gentile). The sequence is theologically precise: you cannot have the horizontal without the vertical. Purely social gospels attempt the horizontal reconciliation without dealing with the underlying problem — alienation from God — and therefore cannot produce lasting unity. The cross solves the root issue; the human reconciliation flows from that solution.

“Killing the hostility” — the same cross that kills sin kills the enmity between peoples. The violence that was directed at Christ absorbs the violence that divided humanity.

Three words here repay a closer look.

First, reconcile. The word assumes something that polite religion prefers to leave vague. You do not reconcile parties who were merely unacquainted, or who had drifted apart through busyness and never quite got round to writing. Reconciliation is what is required when there has been real enmity. Paul says it plainly elsewhere: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10). The trouble was never that God was distant and we were confused. There was hostility, and it ran in both directions — our rebellion against him, and his settled opposition to our evil. Which is precisely why the remedy had to be a death and not an explanation.

Second, in one body. Paul does not say that God reconciled us to himself and then, as a separate matter, suggested we might try to get along with one another. The reconciling puts you somewhere. You are not saved privately and afterwards invited to consider joining a church at your convenience, as though the body were an optional extra for the keener sort of Christian. The same act that brings you to God sets you down among people you did not choose. Which is worth recalling on the Sunday when the congregation seems more trouble than it is worth: you did not select these people, and they did not select you. He reconciled us both, in one body, and the arrangement is not open to renegotiation.

Third, and most striking of all, he killed the hostility. Paul does not write that it was soothed, or managed, or reduced to a workable level, or talked through in a series of meetings. It was put to death, the way a living thing is put to death — because that is what hostility is. Not a regrettable atmosphere, but something with a life of its own, which grows when it is fed and routinely outlives the people who first started it. And notice where it died. They took Christ out and killed him; and in the act of being killed, he killed the thing that was killing everybody. The cross is the one place where hostility did its absolute worst and was destroyed by the very thing it did.

All of which lays out a plain path for anyone currently at odds with a brother or sister in his own congregation — which is exactly the situation this verse was written into. The order is not negotiable: vertical first. Go to the cross yourself and look honestly at the size of what was forgiven you there. It is remarkably difficult to keep a grievance at full strength while standing in that particular place, which is the whole point of the servant who was let off ten thousand talents and went straight out to collect a hundred denarii (Matt. 18:23–35). Two people who have each been forgiven an unpayable debt by the same Person will not, in the end, find they have very much left to hold against each other.

verseByVerse.quote: For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near.” Paul is quoting Isaiah, who had promised exactly this: “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isa. 57:19). What was announced by the prophet has now been carried out in person.

But a question sits in that sentence. When did he come and preach to those who were far off? During his earthly ministry Jesus went almost exclusively to Jews; he told the Twelve at one stage to go nowhere among the Gentiles (Matt. 10:5). He did not preach in Ephesus. So how did the Ephesians hear him?

Through his messengers. The coming Paul has in view is the risen Christ arriving in a Gentile city by the mouth of a man he sent — which is how Paul understood his own work. “How are they to hear without someone preaching?” he asks the Romans, and then quotes the same prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” (Rom. 10:14–15; Isa. 52:7). The feet belong to the messenger; the voice belongs to Christ. And that is not a pious flourish. It means that when the gospel is faithfully preached — from a pulpit, or across a kitchen table, or by somebody who is nervous and doing it badly — Christ himself is doing the preaching. The Ephesians never saw him. They heard him.

Now notice who needed the sermon. He preached peace to those far off — and peace to those who were near. The near ones were the covenant people, with the Scriptures, the temple, the sacrifices and the promises. And they needed the identical message. Nearness, it turns out, was not the same thing as peace. Which is worth pressing, because there is a kind of person in every congregation who has never in his life been far off in any social sense: raised in the church, familiar with the songs, at ease with the vocabulary, never once an outsider. Paul’s sentence says that peace had to be preached to him too, and on precisely the same terms. Proximity to the building was never the same as peace with God, and a man may be very near indeed and still need to hear the announcement.

“Access” (prosagōgē) is the word for the right of approach to a king — being ushered into the royal presence by someone with the standing to bring you in. In the ancient world you did not walk into a throne room uninvited. Now Jew and Gentile alike come before the Father through the same Christ and in the same Spirit. The Trinity is the very architecture of inclusion: access is through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father.

Why “in one Spirit” and not simply “through Christ”? Because the Spirit is the one who makes the access real and present. Christ secured it at the cross — but that was two thousand years ago, outside Jerusalem. How does a believer enter into it now? Not by travelling to Golgotha or by an act of memory, but by the Spirit who indwells us and makes what Christ did then alive in the heart today. “God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Gal. 4:6) — the very cry of “Father” in your prayers is the Spirit at work. And he is the one who gives the standing to approach at all: not our own righteousness carried in as a qualification, but the Spirit of the holy Son indwelling us, our body now his temple (1 Cor. 6:19).

Notice too “one Spirit.” There are not two — one for Jewish believers, one for Gentiles. All come to the Father in the same Spirit, on the same ground, with the same standing; the last distinction is levelled. So whenever a believer prays — however haltingly — something Trinitarian is happening: the Father is approached, through the Son who opened the way, by the Spirit who carries and expresses the prayer from within. Prayer is never a solo cry aimed at a distant deity; the way is open, and it is held open not by our effort but by the Spirit who lives in us (cf. Rom. 8:15–16, 26–27; Heb. 10:19–22).

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So then” gathers up everything from vv.11–18 — the distance, the cross, the peace, the access — into a new identity, in three images that each reverse an exclusion from v.12. The Gentile was a stranger and alien; now they are a fellow citizen, a family member, and a stone in the very building where God dwells. The movement is from edge to centre, from outside to home.

“Members of the household of God” — oikeioi — is warmer than citizenship. Not a tolerated guest on probation but family, belonging to the home: a Father who provides, brothers and sisters in every nation, a home that cannot be taken away (Gal. 6:10; 1 Tim. 3:15). Then Paul shifts to architecture — foundation, cornerstone, holy temple — and it is Temple language on purpose. The new temple is not stone in Jerusalem but a community of people, Jew and Gentile, built on Christ and indwelt by the Spirit, each one a living stone (1 Pet. 2:4–5).

The building rests “on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” — not their personal holiness (they are all long dead) but their testimony, the authoritative word they were commissioned to deliver, now given us in Scripture. They were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, appointed to lay the gospel down in its definitive form (with the New Testament prophets of the founding generation, 3:5; 4:11). Calvin put it plainly: the foundation is the doctrine they preached; move away from it and the whole building falls. This is why sola Scriptura is not a preference but a structural necessity — a church that departs from apostolic teaching does not build higher; it builds on sand.

And “Christ Jesus himself” is the cornerstone (akrogōniaios) — the stone on which everything depends and by which everything is aligned. Misalign it and every stone above it is wrong. Paul is drawing on a deep vein of prophecy: the tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion (Isa. 28:16); “the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 118:22), which Jesus claimed for himself and Peter preached after the resurrection (Acts 4:11); and the same stone that upholds the building is “a stone of stumbling” to those who reject him (Isa. 8:14; 1 Pet. 2:6–8). The builders said, “this one does not fit”; God said, “this one holds everything together.” A church truly built on him will be aligned to him — in doctrine, worship, and love; drift from the cornerstone and it drifts from its own foundation (cf. 1 Cor. 3:11).

Three of those images repay pressing, because each one meant something concrete to people living in that city.

Start with fellow citizens. We hear it as a mild civic word; in Ephesus it was anything but. Roman citizenship was the most prized status in the empire, carrying legal protection, exemption from certain punishments, and the right of appeal to Caesar himself. Paul used his own twice, to considerable effect. He stopped a flogging while the straps were being tied simply by asking whether it was lawful to scourge a Roman who had not been condemned — and the officer, badly shaken, admitted that he had bought his citizenship “for a large sum”, to which Paul replied that he had been born one (Acts 22:25–29). Now set that beside what he is telling these Gentiles. They have been made citizens of a commonwealth beside which Rome is a temporary local arrangement, and they did not purchase it at any price. They were born into it. Our citizenship, as he writes to another Roman colony, is in heaven (Phil. 3:20).

Then the cornerstone, and it is worth knowing exactly what that stone did. It was laid first, at the corner, cut and squared with enormous care — and every other stone in the building took its line and its level from that one. The mason did not measure each new stone against the stone below it; he measured against the corner. Which is why an error there is never a small error. A wall built off a crooked corner is wrong all the way up, it becomes more obviously wrong the higher it rises, and you cannot put it right by adjusting the top. That is precisely how churches drift, and almost never by one dramatic decision. It happens by quietly beginning to take the line from something other than Christ — the founder’s personality, the denomination’s habits, the instincts of the surrounding culture, the preferences of whoever gives the most. Every stone laid after that looks perfectly good on its own, and is out of true.

And do not miss what you are in this picture. Not a visitor admiring the architecture, but a stone in the wall. Peter says it outright: living stones, being built into a spiritual house (1 Pet. 2:5). A stone in a wall is shaped so that it fits the stones beside it. It carries weight, and weight is carried upon it. It cannot be quietly removed without leaving a hole that everybody can see. Which is a considerable distance from what most people mean by church membership. You are not an audience that has been generously admitted to the building. You are load-bearing — and a stone lying on its own in a field, however fine a stone it may be, is not yet part of anything at all.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends the chapter with something architecturally impossible: a building that grows. The word auxei is used elsewhere for the growth of a body or a plant. Buildings do not grow; bodies do — and he mixes the metaphors deliberately, because neither alone can say what he means.

The Temple language — foundation, cornerstone, holy temple — tells us what the church is: the new place where God dwells on earth, built of living stones. It carries weight, permanence, and above all, God is here. But then he says the structure “grows,” and suddenly we are in biology, not architecture: the church is not a finished monument to be maintained but a living thing, still becoming what it is meant to be, still being fitted together by the Spirit (he will develop this in 4:15–16). He needs both images: the building gives the church its solidity, the body its vitality. With only the first it turns rigid and institutional; with only the second, shapeless and rootless. Rooted and growing, fixed and alive.

“Joined together” is sunarmologoumenē, a word found only in Ephesians (again in 4:16) — precise fitting, each stone set exactly where it belongs and bearing on what is next to it. There are no spare stones in this building, no redundant members in this body (cf. 1 Pet. 2:4–5).

Both halves of the impossibility are worth feeling, because a church goes wrong in exactly two directions, and each one is simply the loss of a metaphor.

Lose the growing and you are left with a building and nothing else: a congregation beautifully maintained in which nothing whatever happens. The fabric is sound, the order of service has not altered in thirty years, the accounts are impeccable, and the whole thing has begun to resemble the sort of place kept open by a heritage trust so that visitors may admire the windows. Lose the building and you get the opposite failure: energy without shape, a movement that generates a great deal of warmth for about five years and then discovers it has no foundation under it and nothing solid to hand anybody. Paul will not have either. Rooted and growing. Fixed and alive.

Now notice the verb, which does its work quietly: the structure is being joined together. Present tense, and passive. It is going on now, and it is being done to the stones rather than by them. No stone in a wall ever manoeuvred itself into position, and not one of them chose its neighbours — which is worth remembering when the people on either side of you are not the people you would have picked. They did not pick you either. Neither of you is the mason.

And here is a test you can run on yourself this week, because sunarmologoumenē means precisely fitted — every stone cut so that it bears on the stones beside it. Ask two questions. Is there anybody in your congregation actually bearing weight on you — somebody for whom your absence would be a practical problem and not merely a gap in a pew? And whose weight are you carrying? If the honest answer to both is nobody, then whatever else may be true, you are not yet joined into the wall. You are a stone resting against it. The difference is invisible from the road and total in a storm.

Finally, notice that the building is unfinished, and that Paul states this as a fact rather than an apology. It grows into a holy temple; it has not arrived. So when your church disappoints you — and it will, because a growing thing is always partly unformed — you are not looking at a ruin. You are standing on a building site. The dust and the noise and the half-built walls are not evidence that the project has failed. They are evidence that it is still going on, and that the Builder has not left.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes on five words holding God’s whole ambition for his people: a dwelling place for God. Not a place where people come to find him, but where he himself takes up residence — actually, personally at home. And it raises a wonder: why would the God who fills all things (1:23) want a dwelling place?

Because he has always longed to dwell among his people. It is a thread running the length of Scripture. He walked with Adam in the garden (Gen. 3:8); when sin shattered that, he told Israel to build the Tabernacle “that I may dwell in their midst” (Exod. 25:8) — the word shakan gives us Shekinah, his settling, glorious presence. That glory filled the Tabernacle and later Solomon’s Temple so completely that no one could stand to minister (Exod. 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). He did not merely receive honour there; he moved in. Then came the catastrophe: because of Israel’s idolatry, Ezekiel watched the glory depart the Temple, slowly, reluctantly (Ezek. 10–11) — and the deepest wound was not the Babylonian army but the presence leaving before it came. Yet Ezekiel was given a promise: the glory would return (Ezek. 43:1–5; and the city’s new name, “The Lord is there,” 48:35).

And it returned in a form no one expected. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” — skēnoō, tabernacled, pitched his tent — “and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The Shekinah came back, not to a building of stone but to a body. Then at Pentecost the Spirit descended not on a temple but on people, tongues of fire resting on each one (Acts 2:3) — God moving in again, now into his people. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). It is “by the Spirit” because the Spirit is the mode of God’s indwelling in this age — the living presence of God within the community that gathers, prays, suffers, and loves.

And here is the staggering thing: God wanted a dwelling place, and he chose not a cathedral or a holy mountain but broken, forgiven, still-being-sanctified people. The ordinary congregation on a Sunday morning, with all its unfinished edges, is the dwelling place of the living God — not when it becomes worthy enough, but now. John Stott called the meeting of these last verses one of the most breathtaking things in all of Paul: that the cosmic temple God is building and the local congregation of ordinary believers are the same thing. You are not a spectator. You are a stone in the dwelling place of God on earth (cf. Rev. 21:3).

Two things before the chapter closes. The first is the tense, which is easy to read straight past: you are being built together. Not have been, finally and tidily. It is present, continuous and passive — happening now, and happening to you rather than by you. Nobody in this building put himself there.

The second is what this does to the search most of us have been on. Almost everyone who has ever wanted God has gone looking for his presence somewhere: a place, a view, a piece of music, a conference, a certain quality of silence early in the morning. That hunger is not silly and it is not modern. It is the oldest ache there is. It began on the afternoon when two people heard God walking in the garden and hid from him, and every human being since has carried the memory of a presence he cannot quite locate. But notice the address Paul gives. Not a mountain, not a building, not an atmosphere — a people. God has moved into a congregation.

Which makes an ordinary Sunday a rather more serious business than it looks. The people sitting near you — the awkward ones, the one who talks too long afterwards, the family whose children never sit still — are not the setting in which you might have an encounter with God. They are, together, the place where he has chosen to live. So if you have been looking for his presence and finding it thin, it is worth asking honestly when you last looked for it among the people he actually indwells, rather than in the half-hour of music beforehand.

And see how far the chapter has travelled to say it. It opened with corpses, walking in step with the world and following the prince of the power of the air. It ends with those same people as the house God lives in. That is the distance grace covers — and it covers it in twenty-two verses.

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ,
