The Reformers consistently emphasised that doctrinal unity and relational unity are inseparable. The sevenfold "one" of vv.4–6 grounds the relational unity of vv.2–3 in doctrinal reality. We are not called to unity by ignoring our differences or pretending that doctrine doesn't matter. We are called to unity because there is genuinely one Lord, one faith, one baptism — and the body that confesses these things is, by that very confession, one. Preserving this unity is not sentimentality; it is theological faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was the most socially diverse community in the city. Former Artemis worshippers, Jewish converts, Greek philosophers, slaves and freedmen, wealthy merchants and harbour workers — all brought together by the preaching of the gospel. The centrifugal forces were enormous. Every human instinct would have been to fracture along existing social fault lines. Paul's "therefore" connects the unity he calls for directly to the cosmic reality of chapter 2: the wall has already come down. The body is already one. Now: walk like it. Bear with one another. Choose the humility that makes room for people unlike you. This was not a small ask in first-century Ephesus.

Now: The church in our age is under intense pressure to fragment — along political lines, cultural lines, worship-style lines, theological nuance lines. The market logic of contemporary Christianity encourages us to shop for churches that suit our preferences, reinforcing the very homogeneity that Paul's vision challenges. Against this, Ephesians 4:1–6 calls the church to a costly unity rooted not in shared preference but in shared confession: one Lord, one faith, one baptism. The local church that perseveres through its internal differences — that chooses patient, humble, forbearing love over the easier path of fragmentation — is doing something more theologically significant than it knows. It is bearing witness to the one God who is over all and through all and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Walk in a manner worthy of the calling” — this is the banner over the whole second half of the letter; everything in chapters 4–6 unfolds it. Axios literally means “of equal weight,” like the two pans of a balance scale: the life should be the equal-weight expression of the calling. The calling has been described in chapters 1–3; the walk is that calling lived out. The gap between the calling and the walk is the space in which sanctification happens.

And notice who issues the summons: “a prisoner for the Lord.” Paul’s authority to urge is grounded in his suffering for the gospel — he is not a comfortable advisor but a man in chains for what he is about to ask of them. The moral weight of the appeal is proportional to the cost the appellant has paid.

Feel the turn that has just happened, because it is the sharpest in the letter. For three chapters Paul has issued no commands at all — not one. He has only been describing: chosen, redeemed, sealed, made alive, raised, seated, reconciled, built, indwelt. Then a doxology. And now at last the first imperative of the epistle arrives, and given the size of what has gone before it you might expect something towering. What arrives is: walk.

It is the most pedestrian verb available, and it is chosen deliberately. Paul uses it over and over to organise everything that follows — you once walked that way (2:2), now walk in these good works (2:10), walk worthy (4:1), no longer walk as the Gentiles do (4:17), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), look carefully how you walk (5:15). Walking is what a person does all day without thinking about it. It is not an event. Nobody schedules it, nobody photographs it, and it cannot be done in bursts. Which tells you where the Christian life is actually located: not in the peaks, but in the ordinary going-along of an ordinary week.

Then the word worthy, which needs a guard, because it is easily misheard as earning — and the man who wrote 2:8–9 is not quietly reopening that account four chapters later. Axios is a merchant’s word, the picture of a balance: two pans, the goods in one answered by the weights in the other. Notice which pan you are being asked to attend to. You cannot add anything whatever to the calling side. It is fixed, and it was filled by God before the world was made. You are simply being asked to bring your side up to correspond. A son who bears the family name worthily is not earning the name; he already has it, irrevocably, and nothing he does today will win it or lose it. He is being asked to live like a man who has it.

And notice, finally, who is doing the asking. A prisoner. The man urging you to walk is a man whose own walking has been reduced to the length of a cell. He is not issuing this from a comfortable study. He is asking others to do freely the very thing that has been taken from him — which may be why he asks so gently, and why the word he reaches for is not command but urge.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These four qualities are not a character sketch in the abstract; they are the specific graces by which the unity of v.3 is kept — Paul’s sentence runs unbroken from “walk worthy” to “maintain the unity.” They are the ligaments of peace. Humility was not a virtue in the Greco-Roman world — it described the servile posture of a slave. Paul redefines it as the foundational Christian character; Jesus modelled it at the washing of feet and on the cross. Gentleness is not weakness but controlled strength — power that has chosen to restrain itself for the sake of another.

Patience is long-suffering toward people, not just circumstances. “Bearing with one another” — the word means to put up with, to hold the weight of another’s difficulty. Love is what makes the others sustainable: without it, humility becomes self-abasement, gentleness becomes passivity, and patience becomes resentment.

Take them one at a time, though, because as a list they read like a character reference, and in practice they are considerably more awkward than that.

Gentleness (prautēs) was used of a horse broken to the bridle. The animal has lost none of its strength — that was never the object — but the strength now answers to a hand other than its own. Which is why it is not the same thing as being mild-mannered. A naturally timid man is not gentle in this sense; he simply has nothing needing restraint. Gentleness is what strength looks like once it has been brought under command.

And then the one that does the real work: bearing with one another. The word means to put up with, to carry the weight of. Notice that Paul does not say bear with the difficulties, or the circumstances, or the world outside. He says bear with one another — so the weight in question is other Christians. Make it concrete. It is the man who tells you the same story every time you meet him. The woman who is late to everything and always has a reason. The one whose theology is slightly off and who would like to discuss it after the service, at length. The person who takes twenty minutes to say what needed three. Nobody in that list is sinning. They are simply heavy, in the particular way that people are heavy, and the instruction is to pick the weight up and keep walking.

Which yields a test worth running honestly, because it stings. Everybody reading a verse like this instinctively casts himself as the one doing the bearing. So turn it round: who in your congregation is bearing with you? Somebody is. There is a person who finds your manner difficult, your opinions tiring, your particular blind spot wearing — and who has decided, quietly and without ever telling you, to put up with it and go on loving you anyway. You are somebody’s Wednesday morning. The moment that lands is usually the moment humility stops being a doctrine and becomes possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Maintain” — not create or achieve but guard and preserve. The unity already exists (vv. 4–6 will describe it); the calling is to not break it. “The bond of peace” — peace is the ligament that ties the members together; there is no visible unity without peace between persons.

“Eager” means urgent effort, zealous application. Unity is a gift of the Spirit, but maintaining it in a fallen world — among people who disagree, hurt each other, have different preferences, carry different wounds — requires everything we have (cf. John 17:21).

Everything turns on that first word, so it is worth saying plainly what it rules out. You are not being asked to build unity. You could not; it is not the sort of thing that can be manufactured. Paul says maintain — guard, keep, preserve — because the unity already exists, made by the Spirit, and the only live question is whether you will damage it. It is the difference between founding a family and not wrecking one. Nobody creates his own family. He simply finds himself in it, and what remains to be settled is how he behaves toward people he did not select.

And notice what maintenance actually consists of, because it is thoroughly unglamorous. Nothing is maintained by enthusiasm. A house is maintained by somebody clearing the gutters in November; a marriage by two people apologising rather more often than they would like. The word behind “eager” (spoudazontes) carries urgency and hard effort — make it your business, hurry to it. The unity is a gift; the keeping of it is work.

Then be concrete about what damages it, because we imagine the threat is doctrinal and it very seldom is. Churches do not, as a rule, divide over the person of Christ. They divide over a message that was never returned, a decision taken without consulting somebody who expected to be consulted, a remark repeated to the wrong person, a slight at the door that was probably not even intended. The breach is almost never theological at the point of origin. Theology gets recruited afterwards, to give the wound a respectable name.

Which produces a test with a name attached to it. The bond of peace is never broken in the abstract; it breaks between two particular people. So: is there anybody in your congregation with whom you are not at present at peace — someone you avoid at coffee, or would rather not sit near, or whose name produces a small tightening when you hear it? That is where this verse is addressed, and no quantity of general goodwill toward the church covers it. Paul is not asking you to feel unified. He is asking you to go and repair one specific ligament.

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sevenfold confession is Trinitarian in structure: one Spirit (v.4), one Lord/Christ (v.5), one God and Father (v.6). “One body” — the church is not a collection of individuals but a single organism. “One Spirit” — the same Spirit who sealed every believer indwells the whole without division. “One hope” — the final, eternal destiny of all believers is identical; we are all running toward the same finish line. (Eschatological is simply the theological word for “having to do with the last things — the resurrection, the return of Christ, the new creation”; you will meet it often.) “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” — faith and baptism are not personal achievements but marks of belonging to the one Lord who claimed his people. The unity Paul urges in vv.1–3 is not created by human effort; it is the visible expression of a unity grounded in the very life of the triune God.

And that Trinitarian structure matters, because it means Christian unity is not merely organisational or emotional but theological: we are one because the Father, Son, and Spirit are one, and we are caught up into that life. The church that divides and splinters over secondary matters is acting against its own deepest nature — the three-person God is the pattern, the one body is meant to reflect it, and when the church is genuinely united it displays something of the character of God himself.

Count them as you read: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father. Seven times in three verses Paul strikes the same note. He is not writing elegantly here; he is hammering. And the effect of a list like that is to fix in the mind the sheer scale of what is already held in common, before any question of difference is allowed to come up at all.

So here is a test, and it takes about a minute. Bring to mind the last serious disagreement you watched in a church — the one that cooled a friendship, or emptied a few seats, or is still being carefully not mentioned. Now run it against Paul’s seven. Was it about the one body? The one Spirit? The one hope, the one Lord, the one faith, the one baptism, the one Father? For most disagreements in most churches the honest answer is that the subject does not appear anywhere on the list. The music. The timing. The building. The way a decision was communicated. The preferred translation. A political instinct. None of those is nothing, and some of them matter a good deal — but not one of them is load-bearing, and Paul has just named seven things that are.

And take the one hope personally, because there is an edge on it. The same finish line means the same finishing group. The people you find hardest in your congregation are not a temporary arrangement you will be relieved of at the end. They are the people you will be with, in unshadowed friendship, for ever. Which makes the work of learning to love them now look less like a burden and more like an early start on something you are going to be doing for eternity in any case.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sevenfold confession reaches its summit in the Father. Three prepositions describe three modes of his engagement with his world: over all (sovereignty, transcendence), through all (providential working in and through all things), in all (immanent presence). This is not pantheism but the living God who simultaneously transcends, sustains, and indwells his creation and his redeemed people. When the church fractures into factions, it contradicts the nature of the one God who is Father of all his children — which is why the plea for unity (vv. 1–3) is grounded here in the very character of God.

One clarification is needed, because “one God and Father of all” is regularly produced to prove that everybody is a child of God and that all roads lead home. It will not carry that weight, and the context is what settles it. Paul is not surveying humanity in general; he is in the middle of a passage about the church — one body, one Spirit, one hope, one faith, one baptism. The “all” he keeps repeating is the all of the preceding chapters: Jew and Gentile together, the two made one, the wall down. That is the astonishing thing he is celebrating, and it is emptied rather than enlarged by being stretched to mean everyone without distinction.

Scripture does speak of God as Father of all in the sense that he made every human being and sustains them — Paul said as much to the Athenians (Acts 17:28) — but it reserves the language of sonship in the saving sense for those who receive Christ: “to all who did receive him… he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). Both are true. Only one of them is being spoken of here.

Then let the three small prepositions do their work, because between them they cover everything there is. Over all — nothing outranks him; there is no committee sitting above this Father. Through all — he is no distant proprietor but the one working in and through every circumstance, including the ones you would never have chosen. In all — he is not merely near his people; he is within them. Over you, at work through your week, and living inside you. Which leaves no position remaining from which anything could reach you without passing him first.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having called the church to unity, Paul introduces the glorious diversity that serves it — and its source is the most unexpected one imaginable: the triumphant, ascended, gift-giving Christ. Paul quotes Psalm 68, a victory psalm describing God ascending Mount Zion after defeating his enemies, distributing plunder to his people. He applies it to Christ: the One who descended to the lowest depths of the earth — to death itself, to the far country of human ruin — and then ascended far above all the heavens, has taken the spoils of his victory and distributed them as gifts to his beloved people. And the gifts are not impersonal endowments. They are people. Christ gives gifted persons to his church — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — as the ongoing fruit of his conquest.

But notice first what Paul calls the grace they carry: not saving grace — that has already been lavished in chapters 1–3 — but enabling grace, grace fitted for service, grace for ministry. And its source is Trinitarian: the gifts are given here by Christ the Son (vv. 7, 11); in 1 Corinthians 12 the same gifts flow from the Spirit (vv. 4, 11) and the Father (v. 6). One generosity, three Persons. The giftedness of every believer is a testimony to the Trinity.

And the ascended Christ who gives these gifts is himself the one who “fills all things” (v. 10) — plēroō ta panta. This is the great fullness theme that pulses through the whole letter: the church is his fullness (1:23), the goal of every believer is to be filled with all the fullness of God (3:19), the target of every ministry is the fullness of Christ (4:13). The mission of the exalted Lord is to fill all of creation with his presence, his glory, his life. The church is the first instalment of that filling. To serve in this body is to participate in the most significant project in the universe.

The four gifted offices — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — are not interchangeable. The apostles and prophets belong to the foundational era: they laid the once-for-all deposit of Scripture and revelation on which the whole church stands. The evangelists press outward to where the gospel has not yet reached. The pastor-teachers build up what remains, week by week, year by year, through patient feeding of the word. Each equips the saints in their own way: through the apostolic Scriptures, through the whole counsel of God applied to conscience and life, through training every member to be a witness, through the slow, faithful formation of souls.

And the purpose of this equipping subverts every instinct toward a passive, receiver-only congregation. The saints do the ministry; the gifted leaders equip the saints to do it. The congregation is not the audience; it is the army. The pastor is not the performer; he is the trainer. Diakonia — service — belongs to every member: serving the poor, encouraging the struggling, teaching and discipling one another, praying, giving, witnessing. No gift is too small. No calling too ordinary. The woman who visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home for a small group, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate — all are building the body of Christ.

The goal is breathtaking: unity of the faith, full knowledge of the Son of God, mature manhood, nothing less than the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (v. 13). Not a few exceptional souls reaching great heights, but the whole body — every member — growing together toward the complete image of Christ. This growth is mature, not merely numerical. It is deep, not merely wide. It means speaking the truth in love — not merely in a pleasant tone, but with the costly, goal-directed love that aims at the health of the other person and the glory of Christ, the love that risks the relationship for the sake of the soul (cf. Prov. 27:6; Gal. 4:16).

The result, when every part is working properly, is a body that builds itself up in love (v. 16): growing more mature, more loving, and more attractive to a watching world. Most of this growth is invisible — the unseen ligament, the quiet conversation, the faithful prayer. But it is real, and it is aimed at the most glorious end imaginable: a church that together reflects the full stature of Jesus Christ, the one who fills all things, until God is all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascended Christ and the Equipping Ministry

The passage grounds all ministry in the ascension of Christ — a movement of Pauline theology that is often underemphasised. It is the ascended Christ who gives gifts to His church. The one who has "ascended far above all the heavens" (v.10) is also the one who "fills all things" — present everywhere, sovereign over all, distributing gifts according to His wisdom and His grace. Ministry is not primarily a human enterprise; it is a dimension of the ongoing, active reign of the risen and ascended King.

The list of gifted persons — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — has generated significant debate about which offices are permanent and which ceased with the apostolic age. The Reformed tradition has consistently held that the foundational offices (apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:20) were unique to the founding of the church, while the equipping offices (evangelists, pastor-teachers) continue throughout the church's history. What remains constant in every age is the purpose: equipping the saints for ministry until the whole body reaches the fullness of Christ.

The metaphor of the body in vv.15–16 is Paul's most developed statement of mutual ministry. The body grows "when each part is working properly" — not when a few parts are exceptionally active while the rest remain passive, but when every member is fulfilling their function. This is the vision of a church in which every person is a minister — not because every person preaches, but because every person contributes the grace-gift they have received to the building up of the whole. The body that achieves this grows toward Christ in every way. The body that fails at this — where a few do everything and the many receive — stunts its own growth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had known extraordinary leadership — Paul himself had spent three years there, and the elders he had appointed knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now Paul is gone, and his letter is itself an act of equipping: preparing the church to continue faithfully without his physical presence. The gifted leaders he describes in vv.11–12 are, in the first instance, the elders and teachers of the Ephesian church — men charged with the immense responsibility of preparing every member for a ministry that would build the body in Paul's absence. This was not a programme; it was a pastoral theology applied to a real community facing real challenges.

Now: The consumer church — where the congregation pays for spiritual services delivered by professional clergy — is the precise opposite of Paul's vision. It produces spiritual infants who cannot feed themselves, who are vulnerable to every wind of doctrine, who have no sense of their own giftedness or their own call to ministry. The equipping church — where gifted leaders deliberately, systematically invest in the ministry capacity of every member — produces a body that is robust, maturing, and growing in love. The question for every church leader is not "How well am I performing?" but "How well am I equipping?" And the question for every member is not "Am I being fed?" but "Am I contributing?"

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “but” is a pivot from the corporate unity of verses 1–6 to individual gifting. Diversity within unity. Hekastō — to each one, without exception. No member of the body is ungifted. The measure is determined by Christ; he gives as he sovereignly wills. This is not earned, not developed from natural talent alone, but graciously bestowed by the ascended Lord.

Notice carefully what Paul calls it: grace. But this is not saving grace — the grace of justification already lavished on the Ephesians in chapters 1–2. This is enabling grace: grace fitted for service, grace that equips each member to fulfil their particular calling in the body. The same word, but a distinct work. God’s grace does not stop at the threshold of salvation; it floods every room of the Christian life, including the room of ministry.

And mark the Trinitarian richness here. Paul says the gifts are given by Christ (v. 7, cf. v. 11 “he gave”). Yet in 1 Corinthians 12, the same gifts are distributed by the Spirit (vv. 4, 11) and their diversity traced to the Father (v. 6). Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — one divine generosity, flowing from three Persons. The giftedness of the church is itself a testimony to the Trinity. cf. 1 Cor. 12:4–6.

Many a believer does not feel gifted. This verse insists otherwise: every believer has received grace for ministry. The question is not “do I have a gift?” but “am I using what Christ has given me?” And whoever uses it is drawing on the inexhaustible generosity of the triune God.

That is the right question, but it needs an answer, because a great many people accept it in principle and still have no idea what theirs actually is.

Notice that the New Testament nowhere suggests you should identify your gift first and begin serving afterwards. It works the other way about, which is a considerable relief, since the modern instinct is to take an inventory and wait for clarity. Begin with what is in front of you. What needs doing in your congregation that nobody is doing? What do you find you genuinely care about — the sort of need you are uncomfortable walking past? What do people keep thanking you for, especially when you thought you had done nothing much? What do others keep asking you to do? Those four questions, answered honestly across a year of ordinary service, will tell you a great deal more than any questionnaire. Gifts are identified in use, the way a muscle is discovered by lifting something.

Then attend to the word measure, because it disposes of the two problems that always attach themselves to this subject. Christ apportions; the measures genuinely differ; and both of the usual reactions are ruled out at a stroke. If your measure is smaller than somebody else’s, you have not been short-changed — it was measured out by the one who knows exactly what he intends to do with you, and envy is finally a complaint about his arithmetic. And if your measure is larger, there is nothing whatever in it to be proud of, because a bigger allocation of something you did not earn is not an achievement. It is simply a larger delivery.

So run the comparison test, which is quick and uncomfortable. Whose gift in your church do you quietly envy? And whose do you quietly regard as not really mattering very much? Both answers point at the same misunderstanding — that these things are possessions to be ranked rather than assignments to be used. Nobody in a body is impressed by the hand and dismissive of the liver. Each is simply doing the thing it was put there for.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes Psalm 68:18 — a song of divine-warrior triumph, celebrating God as the conquering king returning from battle, his defeated enemies in his train, distributing the spoils to his people — and applies it to Christ’s ascension. The cross was the decisive battle; the ascension is the triumphal procession; the gifts to the church are the spoils of war handed out to the victors. As Sinclair Ferguson puts it, the church’s gifts “are not human resources organized for divine ends; they are the plunder of Christ’s victory given to his people.”

And who are the captives led in his train? The very powers that once held us enslaved. Sin, whose penalty he bore, so that it no longer has the last word (Rom. 8:1–3). Death, which he walked into and came out the other side — not abolished yet, but stripped of its sting (1 Cor. 15:54–57; Heb. 2:14–15). The devil and his powers, whom he “disarmed… and put to open shame, by triumphing over them” (Col. 2:15). And the law as a condemning power — not the law itself, which is holy, but its power to condemn, which he bore in our place (Gal. 3:13). Christ is not a victim who survived; he is the conquering general, and every gift in your congregation is loot from the battlefield of Calvary.

One detail rewards a look. The Hebrew of Psalm 68 says the victor “received gifts from men,” but Paul writes “he gave gifts to men.” This is not carelessness. In the ancient triumph, receiving tribute and distributing it to one’s soldiers were two phases of one event, and Paul presses the giving phase because that is his point: the ascended Christ gives to his church. (The Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm already read it as giving.) What was pictured in shadow — a victor ascending and enriching his people — is fulfilled in the Son, who ascended to the Father, received all authority, and poured out gifts, the Spirit foremost (Acts 2:33; Phil. 2:9–11).

Picture the scene Paul is borrowing, because his readers had watched one. A Roman triumph was the most spectacular public event in the ancient world: the victorious general in a chariot with laurel on his head, the army behind him, the standards and treasure of the defeated carried through the streets on carts — and walking in chains, in full view of the crowd, the conquered kings themselves. At the end of it the spoil was distributed. That is the picture. Christ ascending, the powers in chains, and the plunder handed out.

Now find yourself somewhere in that procession, and notice which part you were in. The captives being led are the powers that once held you — sin, death, the devil, the condemning force of the law. But by the account of chapter 2, you were on their side of the parade: dead in trespasses, walking according to the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air. You were not a spectator who happened to have backed the winning general. You were in the camp that lost, and the campaign that broke it was fought for you rather than by you.

Which is why nobody in the New Testament boasts about a spiritual gift, and why boasting about one is so peculiarly absurd. Loot is not an accomplishment. A soldier who spent the battle being carried off the field does not, on receiving his share of the spoil, deliver a speech about his contribution. Everything in your congregation that actually works — the teaching, the hospitality, the administration nobody notices, the person who is unaccountably good with the dying — is plunder from a battle in which we were, at best, the objects of the rescue.

So take the gift seriously and yourself lightly. It came off a battlefield, it was bought at a price you did not pay, and it was put into your hands by a general who went down into the ground to get it.

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pauses on a logical point: ascent presupposes descent. The one who went up is the one who first went down — the eternal Son descending into the humiliation of incarnation, into the full depth of human experience, into death itself. As Sproul said, there is no depth of human experience where Christ has not gone, and from which he has not returned victorious. (“The lower parts of the earth” has been read either as the earth itself — the descent being the incarnation — or as the realm of the dead, so that the descent includes his death; either way the point holds: exaltation to the highest place presupposes willingness to descend to the lowest.)

Because the verse speaks of Christ “descending,” many a reader ties it at once to the line in the Apostles’ Creed — “he descended into hell” — and to the picture of Christ, between his death and resurrection, going down to preach to imprisoned souls. It is worth saying plainly where that idea does and does not rest. It does not rest here. Paul’s “lower regions” most likely means either the earth itself, so that the descent is the incarnation — the Son coming down to be born — or, if it reaches to death, then the grave; not a tour of the underworld. The “harrowing of hell” picture leans chiefly on one difficult and much-debated verse, “he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison” (1 Pet. 3:19), over which careful Christians have long disagreed, and it is not settled enough to build a doctrine on. So do not read a descent into hell out of this text; Paul is not mapping the afterlife but tracing the sweep from the lowest place to the highest. And the creedal line itself need not mean a rescue mission through hell: Calvin and much of the Reformed tradition took “descended into hell” to mean the depth of Christ’s suffering — that on the cross he bore the very anguish and God-forsakenness of hell in our place. A churchgoer can say the words with full meaning and import no legend. What Paul does press is the reach of it: there is no depth the Son did not go down into, and therefore none from which he cannot lift you.

And the purpose is that “he might fill all things.” The word fill courses through this letter like a river — the church “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (1:23), the prayer to “be filled with all the fullness of God” (3:19), the goal of “the fullness of Christ” (4:13), the command to “be filled with the Spirit” (5:18). It is the theological pulse of Ephesians: the mission of the ascended Christ is to fill all creation with his glory and life. He fills the cosmos as Lord, the church as Head, each believer by his Spirit — not pantheism (he does not become creation), but a universal presence that leaves nothing outside his reach, moving toward the day when God is “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

And this is breathtaking comfort. He who filled the far country of death now fills the far country of your suffering. There is no grief so dark, no failure so complete, no situation so hollow that the filling Christ cannot enter it. The one who fills all things has not overlooked you (cf. Col. 1:17–20).

Before leaving the descent, let it be counted out rather than summarised, because “he descended” covers a very long way down and we are inclined to take it in a single word.

From the throne, where he was worshipped without interruption, to a womb. From the womb to a feeding trough in a borrowed stable. From there to a provincial village with a poor reputation, and twenty years in a workshop making door frames and yokes. Then to an itinerant life with nowhere of his own to sleep. To being thought out of his mind by his own family, who came to take him home by force. To a friend’s kiss in a garden at night, and the rest of them running. To a courtyard where the man who had sworn to die with him denied he had ever met him. To a rigged trial, a whipping post, a crown made as a joke. To a public execution reserved for slaves and rebels, stripped, between two criminals. To a cry of dereliction. To a corpse. To a grave with a stone rolled across it.

That is the descent, step by step, and every stair of it goes downward. Now set your own depth beside it. To be misunderstood by the people who ought to know you best — he has been there. To be let down by the friends you were counting on, at precisely the moment it mattered — he has been there. To pray in real anguish and get silence back — he has been there. To be shamed publicly and unjustly, to be physically broken, to die: every one of those is a place he has already stood, and he did not visit any of them as an observer.

So try naming, honestly, the one place you suspect he cannot reach — the particular thing about your situation that feels beyond the range of anybody’s sympathy, his included. Then hold it against that list. The whole force of Paul’s parenthesis is that the one who now fills all things earned the right to do so by going underneath all things first. There is no cellar in your life with a floor lower than the one he has already stood on.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are not gifts so much as gifted persons — Christ gives people to the church. He lists apostles and prophets first (the foundation, 2:20), then the continuing offices of evangelist and pastor-teacher. The apostles were those personally commissioned by the risen Christ, eyewitnesses of the resurrection, with authority to speak and write his word with binding force (Paul among them, though he had not walked with Jesus, 1 Cor. 15:8). Their role was foundational and unrepeatable — the New Testament is their legacy — and a foundation is laid once; there are no apostles today in that primary sense. The prophets here are New Testament prophets who received direct revelation before the canon was complete; with its closing, that revelatory function ceased, though the gift of proclamation — forthtelling — continues in every preacher who opens the word.

The evangelists were gifted to carry the gospel to those who had not heard — frontier workers like Philip and Timothy, breaking ground and planting churches; the church needs them in every generation. And the shepherds and teachers are almost certainly one office (the Greek groups them): the pastor-teacher who tends the flock by feeding it the word — care and protection joined to faithful, nourishing exposition (John 10:11–14; 1 Pet. 5:1–4).

So did the apostles and prophets carry on after the Bible was written? No — those were once-for-all, foundational offices. But Christ still gives the church evangelists to take the gospel where it has not been heard, and pastor-teachers to preach and shepherd Sunday by Sunday. Both are alive and well today. Every faithful pastor, every gospel-carrying missionary, is a gift from the ascended Christ — he did not leave his people without the people they need. A reason to honour and pray for the pastors he has given you.

And notice exactly what he gave, because it is the practical edge of the whole verse. Not programmes, not structures, not a curriculum — people. When the ascended Lord provided for the needs of his church, the provision arrived with a name, a family, a limited constitution, and a telephone that rings at inconvenient hours.

That cuts in two directions and both are worth feeling. It means the gift is far better than any resource could be, because a book cannot sit with you in a hospital corridor at two in the morning, and a recording cannot notice that you have stopped coming. And it means the gift will disappoint you in ways a resource never would. Your pastor has a temperament, and some of it will grate. He has blind spots, and you will find them. He will preach a thin sermon in the very month you needed a good one. Congregations often deal with this by concluding that the wrong man was given, when what has actually happened is that a man was given, which was the arrangement from the beginning.

So here is a test, and it is uncomfortably easy to answer. When did you last pray for your pastor by name — not as a category at the end of a list, but deliberately, about the specific things you know he is carrying? And when did you last tell him something particular that helped? Most ministers live on a diet of general encouragement and precise criticism. The criticism arrives with details, dates and examples; the encouragement arrives as “nice sermon” at the door. Reverse those two for a year in your congregation and you would scarcely recognise the man at the end of it.

Christ did not leave his people to work it out from a manual. He gave them people — and then told the people they were given to, to look after them.

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is one of the most transformative verses in all of ecclesiology. The purpose of the gifted leaders is not to do the ministry for the saints but to equip them — the word (katartizō) is used for mending nets and setting bones, fitting a thing for its proper function — so that they do the work of ministry. The result Paul envisions is a congregation of ministers, not a minister with a congregation: every member fitted for their function, every joint contributing (v.16). Pastoral ministry is not performance but preparation (cf. Rom. 12:4–5; 1 Cor. 12:7).

And the ministry the members do is not confined to pulpit or platform. Paul uses the broad word diakonia — service — deliberately: practical care for the sick, the widow, the stranger (Matt. 25:35–36; James 1:27); encouragement that strengthens faith (Heb. 3:13); teaching and discipling, older saints and younger, one to one (2 Tim. 2:2; Titus 2:3–5); witness to neighbours and colleagues (1 Pet. 3:15); intercession (Eph. 6:18); and generous giving that funds the work (2 Cor. 9:6–8). No gift is too small and no calling too ordinary to be included. The woman who visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate — all are doing the work of ministry.

And the goal is “building up the body of Christ” — an architectural word (oikodomē) for a building that is somehow alive and grows. It means at least three things together: numerical growth, as the lost are converted and welcomed (Acts 2:47); maturity and depth, each member growing toward “the fullness of Christ” (v.13); and unity, the parts fitted and working together in love (v.16). To serve one another in the smallest act of diakonia is to share in the very purpose of God for history, for the church is “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (1:23).

One thing should be said openly, because a reader with an older Bible will notice it at once. The whole weight of the paragraph above rests on where the commas fall, and the translations do not agree.

The King James has it: “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ” — three commas, three parallel tasks, and all three belonging to the apostles, prophets, evangelists and pastors of verse 11. Read that way, the ministry is what the leaders do. The modern versions drop the second comma: he gave leaders to equip the saints for the work of ministry — and now the ministry is what the saints do, with the leaders preparing them to do it. That comma has been called the most consequential in the history of the church, which is not much of an exaggeration; a great deal of what people simply assume about clergy and congregation follows from it.

The modern reading has the better case, and the reason survives translation. Paul changes his preposition. The first phrase uses one word (pros — toward, with a view to) and the two that follow use another (eis — resulting in, leading to). Three genuinely parallel items would naturally have taken the same preposition three times over. The shift marks a step down instead: leaders are given with a view to equipping the saints, which results in the work of ministry, which results in the body being built up. The saints are not the objects of the ministry. They are the ones performing it.

Which yields an uncomfortable way of measuring a church. We instinctively assess a congregation by the output of its minister — was the sermon good, is he a capable leader, does he visit enough. This verse measures something else entirely: are the members functioning? So ask it plainly. If your pastor were removed from your church for six months, how much of its actual ministry would simply stop? In some congregations the honest answer is nearly all of it — and that is not a compliment to the pastor. It is precisely the condition this verse was written to prevent.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal is partly future — maturity is a direction of travel, not a destination reached in this life — and Paul stacks four phrases for it, four angles on one glorious end. “The unity of the faith” is not the unity of tolerance that smooths over difference by indifference to truth, but the deep agreement that comes when the whole body holds the faith — the apostolic gospel received and confessed together (Jude 3). “The knowledge of the Son of God” is epignōsis — not intellectual acquaintance but full, personal, transforming knowing; Calvin held that the whole Christian life is a progressive knowing of Christ, and we are never so advanced that we do not need to know him better. The aim of all ministry is not a more informed congregation but one more deeply captivated by Jesus himself.

“Mature manhood” (andra teleion) is corporate — the whole church together reaching the stature of a grown person; maturity here is not the absence of struggle but the presence of stability, a faith no longer easily capsized. And the standard is “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” — the most breathtaking phrase of the four. Not the finest elder in your church, not some ideal of virtue, but Christ himself in his fullness (plērōma again, 1:23). The destination is a people who, together, look like Christ. It will not be fully reached until the last day, but it is the real goal, not a figure of speech.

The alternative is the instability of v.14: children “tossed to and fro by the waves,” carried about by every wind of doctrine. “Cunning” there is panourgia, the craftiness of the serpent in Genesis — and false teaching has always dressed itself in theological-sounding words. The lasting defence is not mainly knowing why error is dangerous, but knowing the Son of God more deeply. Doctrinal stability is a fruit of growth, not suspicion.

But picture the alternative he sets against maturity, because the image is very exact: a small boat with nothing whatever to steady it. Tossed by the waves — that is the movement from underneath, the swell of feeling and circumstance. Carried about by every wind — that is the push from outside, whatever happens to be blowing this season. No ballast, no keel, no anchor. A boat in that condition is not steered anywhere at all; it simply goes wherever the water and the air have most recently decided.

What that looks like in practice is recognisable enough. It is the Christian whose convictions can be dated by whatever he last read or listened to. The person who is enthusiastic about a new teacher roughly every eighteen months, and each time it is the thing that has finally made sense of everything. The one who is persuaded by whoever spoke most confidently in the room, on a subject he has never actually examined for himself. None of this requires bad motives. Paul’s word for children is not an insult; it is the description of a stage, and the only tragedy is in staying there.

And notice how error actually arrives, because it never announces itself. Panourgia is the craftiness of the serpent, who opened not with a denial but with a question. Error comes warmly, from people who are likeable and sincere, wrapped around a very large quantity of truth. If it presented itself as error nobody would take it. What makes it dangerous is that nine-tenths of it is right, and the remaining tenth is load-bearing.

So a test, answered honestly rather than defensively. Over the last five years, has your view of something significant shifted more than once — and when you trace back why, was the cause a passage of Scripture you finally understood, or a person you found compelling? Both can move you; only one of them anchors you. And the remedy Paul offers is not to become suspicious of everything, which produces a hard and frightened Christian rather than a mature one. It is to know the Son of God so well that counterfeits declare themselves by contrast — the way a man who handles genuine banknotes all day needs no course in forgery.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alētheuontes en agapē — “truthing in love.” Not just speaking truth but living it, in a setting of love. Truth without love is cold; love without truth is hollow; the maturing church holds both as it grows into its head. The truth Paul means is the gospel truth of vv.13–14 — who Christ is, what he has done, what it means to live in him — the very truth the false teachers are trying to distort, and it must be spoken: in preaching, in correction, in the daily witness of an aligned life (Col. 3:16). And “in love” means far more than a pleasant tone. It is love with a goal: the good of the other, the health of the body, the glory of Christ — speaking truth for someone rather than at them. Love is what separates the surgeon’s scalpel from the bully’s fist; both may cause pain, but only one is aimed at healing. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Prov. 27:6); truth told in love risks the relationship for the sake of the person (Gal. 4:16).

“Grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ.” The phrase “in every way” allows no partial growth — not knowledge while love withers, not zeal while wisdom lags, but doctrine, character, relationships, worship, witness, suffering, all of it moving in one direction: into Christ. He is not merely the model of maturity; he is its substance. To grow up is not to become a more impressive version of yourself but to become more like him, more hidden in him (cf. Col. 2:19; 2 Cor. 3:18).

Then verse 16 — a masterpiece of organic metaphor: from Christ the head “the whole body, joined and held together by every joint,” each part working properly, “makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.” MacArthur calls it the most comprehensive description of church growth in the New Testament. And that growth is at once deeper (toward the fullness of Christ), warmer (built up in love — maturity without growing love is only sophistication), and wider (a body overflowing with such love is itself an instrument of evangelism — “by this all people will know that you are my disciples,” John 13:35).

And notice how it happens: not through the heroics of a few outstanding individuals but through the faithful, ordinary contribution of every part. The encourager who seeks out the one who is struggling. The small group that studies and prays and holds one another under pressure. The older woman discipling a younger (Titus 2:3–5). The congregation that absorbs the cost of a disagreement rather than fracture. The deacon who visits the sick, the giver who funds the missionary, the intercessor who rises early. The ligament is never seen, the joint never applauded — but remove them and the body collapses. These quiet acts are the materials from which Christ is building his church (cf. 1 Cor. 12:21–26).

One thing needs adding, because “speaking the truth in love” is probably the most quoted and most abused phrase in this chapter. It gets used to license the very thing it forbids, and it gets used just as often to excuse never saying anything at all. Both failures are common, and each is comfortable in its own way.

Take the first. A man decides something must be said, says it plainly, and afterwards feels the particular satisfaction of having been faithful — and everybody who heard it knows quite well that the satisfaction was the point. The sentence had been composed in advance. It arrived with a certain relish. Nothing about it cost the speaker anything, and the person on the receiving end was left with no way forward. That is not truth in love. It is candour with a scriptural warrant pinned to the front of it.

Then the second, which is far more respectable and does a great deal more damage in most congregations. Somebody is drifting, or a marriage is quietly failing, or a man’s temper is frightening his children — and nobody says a word. We call the silence love. It is almost never love. It is the avoidance of an unpleasant conversation, and love has simply been recruited to cover for it. If you have belonged to a church for years and have never once said a hard thing to anybody in it, that fact requires a better explanation than gentleness.

Three questions will usually tell you which of the two you are doing, and they take about a minute. Have you prayed for this person more than you have rehearsed the sentence? Will this cost you something, or only them — because the bully’s version is free, while love’s version puts the friendship at risk. And would you be willing for somebody to do this to you next month, about your own blind spot? If the answers come back the wrong way, the trouble is not that you have too much truth. It is that you have not yet enough love to carry it.

And notice where Paul places this. It is the very first thing he names about growing up. Not more study, not more discipline — learning to tell one another the truth in a way that heals. A church of people who can do that will mature. A church that cannot will remain a nursery, however good the preaching.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from theology to the street. “No longer walk as the Gentiles walk.” Not a gentle suggestion — an apostolic command, issued in the Lord’s name. And the reason it must be commanded is itself the warning: becoming a Christian does not automatically remake your habits. The old gravity is still there. You must walk differently, deliberately, because the new life does not run on autopilot.

The diagnosis is sober: a mind cut loose from God loses its anchor. Not its intelligence — its direction. It thinks hard but goes nowhere. The understanding darkens. The heart hardens — not in a single dramatic moment but through the quiet accumulation of small refusals, each making the next a little easier, until the conscience is worn smooth and the soul no longer notices what it has lost. Sensuality, insatiable craving, the futile pursuit of things that cannot satisfy — this is where the road ends. Paul is not describing monsters. He is describing the trajectory of every unrenewed human heart, including the one that used to belong to these Ephesians.

But they have learned Christ. And that changes everything. The old self — the whole person oriented away from God, rotting through deceitful desires — is to be stripped off like a stinking garment. The mind is to be renewed, daily and continuously, by the Spirit working at the deepest level. The new self — a new creation, bearing the restored image of God in genuine righteousness and holiness — is to be put on. This is not self-improvement. It is resurrection applied to daily life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Renewal of the Mind and the New Humanity

The "old self" and "new self" of this passage are not psychological categories — they are eschatological ones. The old self is the Adamic humanity: the self that has inherited Adam's corruption, lives under the dominion of sin, and is "corrupt through deceitful desires" (v.22). The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be "in Christ" is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: "be transformed by the renewal of your mind." The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is "the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in His image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I say and testify in the Lord” — that second word is heavier than it looks. The Greek is martyromai, from martys, “witness” — the root that gives us martyr. It belongs to the solemn, legal register: to call something to witness, to affirm it as under oath. Paul is not offering friendly advice; he is swearing a charge, staking his own witness on it. And that he must issue it at all tells us something: conversion does not automatically make us live as God wills. The old patterns do not vanish overnight; the new life must be deliberately walked.

“No longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.” “Futility” (mataiotēs) means emptiness — the very word the Old Testament uses for idols, “vain things” that cannot see or save or satisfy (Jer. 2:5); and “mind” (nous) is the whole faculty by which a person weighs what is real and decides how to live. So the diagnosis is exact: not merely muddled thinking, but a mind whose every judgment is bent because the thing at its centre is empty. Paul writes to Ephesus, built around the temple of Artemis — a life of praying to stone, buying charms, paying astrologers (Acts 19:19), busy and even religious, but aimed at gods who were not there. And there is the madness of it: a man can pour out his whole life — his worship, his labour, his deepest longing — upon what is, in truth, nothing at all.

Underneath it is a hunger. God made the heart for himself, and, as Augustine prayed, “our heart is restless until it rests in you.” We try to fill that ache with good things — family, work, a hard-earned holiday — gifts of God, every one, but never built to carry the weight of it. This is the whole burden of Ecclesiastes: the Preacher tried pleasure, work, wealth, wisdom, and called it all “vanity” (hevel, a vapour you cannot hold) — and when the book was put into Greek, that refrain was rendered with this very word, mataiotēs. Good things chased without God come up empty. Only the idols have changed clothes: the bigger house, the endless scroll, the next achievement that was finally going to satisfy — plenty of motion, no destination.

And none of this stops at conversion. You are redeemed, and you still catch yourself reaching for the old empty wells, half-believing the next thing will fill you. How do you fight it? Not mainly by gritting your teeth to want less — a hungry heart is not talked out of eating. Thomas Chalmers named the real cure: “the expulsive power of a new affection.” You do not drive out a lesser love by willpower but by a greater one. So when the itch comes — if I just had that, I’d be content — name it: that is the hunger again, and that thing cannot fill it. Preach the truth back to yourself before the craving talks you into it (the daily renewal of the mind, Rom. 12:2). Feed the real hunger at its only true source — the Word, prayer, the Lord’s table, God’s people. And receive the good gifts — your spouse, your work, your Saturday rest — not as gods that must satisfy, but as gifts from a Father who already has.

Set this diagnosis beside its cure and the contrast is exact — Paul even uses the same word. Here the Gentile mind (nous) is futile; to the Romans he pleads, “be transformed by the renewal of your mind” — the renewal of the nous (cf. Rom. 12:2). Same faculty, opposite destinies: what is empty here is the very thing grace makes new. And the renewed mind, Paul adds, now thinks “with sober judgment” (Rom. 12:3) — clear-eyed before God and self, the exact reverse of the darkened, self-deceived understanding of the next verse. The gospel does not merely correct the empty mind; it renews it.

One last thing changes how the whole command feels. You can hear “you must no longer walk” as nothing but duty — I’ve been given much, so I’d better shape up. But God is not calling you out of a good life into a grey one of chores. He is calling you out of the empty life into the full one. The walk Paul commands is not the price of being saved; it is the beauty of it — the life the heart was actually made for. The old way looked like freedom and proved a cage; this way looks like surrender and proves to be the open field (cf. Rom. 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul traces a chain, and the little joining words (“because of the ignorance… due to the hardness”) run from the surface down to the root: the darkened understanding is the visible symptom; beneath it, alienation from the life of God; beneath that, a wilful ignorance; and at the bottom, a hardened heart. The engine, though, runs the other way — the heart hardens first, and everything else follows downstream. This is not random moral failure but the predictable anatomy of a life moving away from God.

Darkened in their understanding — and the form is passive: not that they darkened themselves, but that they have been darkened; behind every eye a man closes against the light stands a judgment he did not administer. This is not stupidity — these people may be brilliant. It is the faculty by which a person decides what is worth living for, so that the needle still swings confidently but points the wrong way. Back then it looked respectable: a man pouring his years into status and the favour of Artemis, and every neighbour nodding that he lived wisely — aimed all the while at gods who were not there. And it looks just as respectable now: a decent, hard-working man pouring his one life into the career, the retirement number, the renovated house, the evenings handed to a screen — nothing scandalous, all reasonable, much of it aimed at a horizon that ends at the grave, while Christ quietly seems optional (Rom. 1:21; 2 Cor. 4:4).

And Paul has already prayed the cure for this exact darkness. To the same church, in the same letter, he asked God to grant “the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know the hope to which he has called you” (cf. Eph. 1:18). Here the understanding is darkened; there the eyes of the heart are enlightened — the same faculty of sight, opposite conditions. And note who throws the switch: not the mind lighting itself, but the Father giving light. The god of this age blinds (2 Cor. 4:4); the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” is the One who shines in the heart (2 Cor. 4:6). What sin darkened, grace floods with day.

But do not draw the wrong conclusion. Paul is not saying work and family are “worldly stuff” that does not matter, as though only church and evangelism counted with God — that is not in the Bible. God invented work before sin entered (Gen. 2:15) and called marriage and family good (Gen. 1:28). The cure was never to do less. The compass was the problem, not the road. Take the very same Monday and change the aim: do the work “as for the Lord and not for men” (Col. 3:23), love your family as a trust rather than a monument to yourself, eat and drink and clock in “all to the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10:31). To the neighbour over the fence nothing looks different; underneath, everything is — the same hands at the same tasks, no longer trying to fill the God-shaped space, but offered back to the God who already fills it.

Alienated from the life of God — there are two kinds of life. There is the life you can measure, breath and heartbeat, which every person has. And there is the deeper life: God’s own life flowing into a soul, the inner man awake and joined to its Maker. Picture a flower cut for the table: on Monday it looks perfect, bright and upright — but cut from its root it is already dying; it simply has not shown yet. That is a person alienated from the life of God — up and about, laughing, working, while cut off from the Root. “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5). And this is the very thing Christ came to reverse: the borrowed heartbeat of a cut flower gives way to life drawn again from the Root — not bare existence, but “life… to the full” (cf. John 10:10).

Beneath that lies ignorance — not for lack of information but the willed not-knowing of a man who keeps shutting his eyes against the sun and then complains that it is night (Rom. 1:21). And at the root, hardness of heart — pōrōsis, a medical word for calcification, hard tissue forming where there should be living flexibility. It is not one dramatic rebellion but the accumulation of small refusals, each making the next easier. Pharaoh is the case study, and the two halves must be held together: again and again he hardened his own heart, and again and again the LORD hardened it — the man hardened himself until God confirmed him in the hardness he had chosen. That is the most frightening sentence a soul can receive: not lightning, but a handing-over, God ceasing to interrupt. Which is why Scripture pleads, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Heb. 3:7–13).

The end of that road is a conscience worn smooth — callous, no longer feeling what it has lost — so that they “give themselves up to sensuality” (aselgeia, appetite with the brakes removed) and grow “greedy to practise every kind of impurity.” The word for greedy (pleonexia) tells the truth of it: indulgence does not satisfy, it inflames; the one who thought freedom lay in removing every limit finds himself enslaved to cravings that cannot be fed (Rom. 1:28). And that very insatiability is the back-handed proof of what the soul was made for: a thirst this deep was never meant for the far country but for the One who says, “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (cf. John 4:14; 6:35) — the appetite that nothing here could fill, answered at last by the only spring that satisfies.

And here, at the root, is the sweetest reversal of all. A heart can harden itself, but it cannot soften itself — calcified tissue does not choose to become supple again. So God pledges to do the one thing the sinner cannot: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (cf. Ezek. 36:26). Not a hard heart lectured into softness, but a new heart given. And because the hardened heart was the engine of the whole descent, when grace turns the root the rest turns with it — the darkened mind, the alienation, the very ignorance answered at a stroke. From a new heart flows a new life.

For you, this chain is a warning, not just a description. None of it begins with a dramatic fall; it begins quietly — a little hardness, a little less sensitivity, a little more drift. The Christian reads it with recognition, not superiority: this was the road we were on. Grace interrupted it. Do not drift back.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But that is not the way you learned Christ.” After the bleak description of vv. 18–19, Paul turns on a dime. That world — darkened, alienated, callous, insatiable — is not what you signed up for. You learned something completely different.

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say “you learned about Christ” or “you learned Christ’s teaching.” He says you learned Christ — a Person, not a curriculum. In the ancient world you learned a philosopher’s ideas; the philosopher himself was just the delivery mechanism. Paul is saying something far more radical: the content of Christian learning is Christ himself. You were not handed a new moral code. You were introduced to a living Person — and knowing him is what changes everything.

And this is no turn of phrase peculiar to Paul. Jesus framed discipleship exactly so: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matt. 11:29) — not learn my system, but learn me; the Teacher is himself the lesson. To be a disciple (mathētēs, literally a learner) was never to master a syllabus but to apprentice to a Person until his life reshapes yours. And where does such learning end? Not in facts stored but in a self remade — until a man can say with Paul, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (cf. Gal. 2:20). That is the far end of learning Christ: not that you know more about him, but that he comes to live his life through you.

This is the sharpest possible contrast with the futile mind of v. 17. The pagan mind drifts because it has no fixed point. The Christian mind has one: a Person who does not change, who is not a theory, who can be known and who makes himself known. That is what you learned. Live like it.

Which raises the obvious question, and it is worth answering, because the difference between learning a subject and learning a person runs straight through the Christian life. Nobody learns a person the way he learns a subject. You cannot come to know somebody by reading a summary of him. It takes time, attention, presence, and a good deal of watching him under pressure — and at the end of it you know something you could never have written down in advance.

So take the ordinary means and use them in that way. Read the Gospels not principally for information but in order to watch him: how he handles interruption, what makes him angry, whom he stops for, how he speaks to people who have failed badly. Pray as conversation rather than recitation — and notice that both of those are simply time spent in company. And obey, because this is the part we habitually leave out. Jesus said that the one who keeps his word is the one to whom he will show himself (cf. John 14:21). Obedience is not the fee charged for knowing him; it is one of the ways the knowing actually happens, since you discover what a person is like chiefly by doing things alongside him.

Then a test, quick and rather revealing. Try to say, in one sentence, what Jesus is like — not what he did, not what he taught, not what he accomplished at the cross, but what he is like to deal with. Most of us can produce a good deal of accurate material under the first three headings and find the fourth unexpectedly hard. That gap is precisely the difference between having learned about him and having learned him.

And it matters, because the manner of the learning shapes the walk. A man handed a rule-book keeps rules badly and is resenting them by Thursday. A man who has come to love a Person finds his behaviour being altered from somewhere further in than his will. Paul is about to spend two chapters telling the Ephesians how to live. He lays this down first, because everything that follows would be impossible on any other footing.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Assuming that you have heard him and were taught in him” — Paul is not doubting their conversion but reminding them what they received. And notice the little word: taught in him, not by him. Had he meant mere agency he could have said “through him.” He writes “in him” — the incorporative “in Christ” language that saturates this letter. The teaching did not arrive from outside as an information transfer, a parcel of facts handed over at arm’s length; it happened within your union with Christ. This is why the futile, darkened mind of vv.17–19 could never arrive here — it operates outside that union — and why what follows is not a new rulebook posted from a distance but instruction from inside the sphere of Christ, able to produce a “new self” (v.24) rather than one more round of futile effort.

“As the truth is in Jesus” — and again the exact words. Not that the truth is Jesus, an equals sign, but that it is in him: found, lodged, given a face in him. And Paul uses the human name deliberately — not “Christ” the title but “Jesus,” the man who walked in Galilee, touched lepers, was crucified under Pilate, and rose. Truth is not an abstract system floating free of a person; it has taken flesh in a specific human life. Hold that, for it sets the axis of the passage: the truth is in Jesus (v.21), the old self is corrupted through deceitful desires (v.22). Truth against deceit — that is the real contest. The old life is not merely naughty; it is a lie whispered to a man about where his happiness lies.

So when you want to know what truth looks like in flesh and blood — how to forgive, how to suffer — you do not consult a definition; you look at Jesus. You could hand a man the dictionary meaning of courage, accurate and bloodless, or point him to the soldier who threw himself on the grenade for his friends — courage with a face. A piano teacher can give you the theory of a sonata, or sit down and play it: “there — that is what it is meant to sound like.” In Jesus the truth about God and about what a human life was made to be stopped being a concept and became a life you can watch. The world says truth is whatever feels right to you; Paul says it is not ours to shape at all, because it is found in a Person who cannot be revised — “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Heb. 13:8; cf. 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put off” — the clothing image was already common in the ancient world, but Paul sharpens it: this is not adjusting your wardrobe but stripping off an entire identity — the whole of who you take yourself to be, your deepest loves and loyalties and habits. And “your old self” is literally “the old man” (as in Rom. 6:6; Col. 3:9) — not the body or the personality but the whole human self as it was before Christ, the person you were in Adam, oriented away from God. It is not a part of you; it is the old you.

Paul says this old self “belongs to your former manner of life,” and the phrasing is deliberate. The old self and the old life are so bound together that you cannot keep one and lose the other. The old way of living is the old self’s natural habitat; if you want to leave the old life behind, the old self must go with it. You cannot keep the old self and expect new behaviour — the root and the fruit come as a package.

And it is “corrupt” — not in the sense of dishonest, but rotting: the word for decay, something actively dying. You do not renovate what is rotting; you put it off. It is corrupting “through deceitful desires” — desires called deceitful because they make promises they cannot keep: this will satisfy you, this will fill the gap. They never do, and with each broken promise the person goes deeper in, feeding on what cannot nourish, slowly consuming himself. James names the lure exactly — each is “lured and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14) — and the believer’s answer is decisive: those who belong to Christ “have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

But how do you put off something as deep as your very self? Not by willpower wrestling a living master to the ground — by faith reckoning on a death already died. “We know that our old self was crucified with him” (Rom. 6:6): in Christ the old man has already been put to death. So to “put off” is not to kill what is thriving but to stop dressing a dead man each morning — to leave off the grave-clothes of a corpse. And it has its answering side: you were not only crucified with Christ but raised with him (cf. Col. 3:1–3), which is why the very next word is not another command to grit your teeth but a promise — be renewed.

One thing more, because “deceitful desires” is exactly the right phrase and we tend to leave it abstract. A desire that deceives makes promises, in words — and it is worth writing the words down, because they are remarkably few and they never vary much. Just this once, and then never again. You have earned this; look at the week you have had. Nobody will ever know. You will feel better afterwards. You can stop whenever you decide to. Everybody does this; you are being ridiculous about it. That is very nearly the whole script. It is not sophisticated and it does not need to be, because it is delivered at the one moment when you are least inclined to examine it.

Then notice what is actually delivered, which is the part nobody rehearses beforehand. Ten minutes afterwards there is no satisfaction to speak of. There is a slight flatness, and the beginning of the wish that it had not happened. The thing that was going to make you feel better has made you feel worse, and the promise has not simply failed — it has left you a little further in than you were before.
